Consumption beta varies through time and cross sectionally due to variation in half-lives and stationary volatilities of the dividend signals. Winner (Loser) stocks exhibit high (low) half-lives and stationary volatilities, and thus exhibit high (low) consumption beta commanding high (low) risk-premium. The model also rationalizes the "momentum crashes" phenomenon discussed in Daniel and Moskowitz (2014). High half-lives of dividend signals in Winners keep their consumption betas low long after recovering from a prolonged economic downturn, while low half-lives in Losers make their consumption betas grow rather quickly. Thus, coming out of a recession, the long Winner/short Loser strategy reduces in consumption beta and, hence, risk-premia.

papers.title: Cross-sectional currency momentum and order flow *
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether high buying pressure is associated with higher crosssectional currency momentum returns. We employ order flows from the spot, forward, and swap markets, as well as the maturities of swap and forward contracts, to construct portfolios based on momentum and buying pressure. We find heterogeneous effects of order flows across instruments and maturities on cross-sectional currency momentum portfolios. High buying pressure in the short-term swap market leads to stronger momentum returns. This pattern is particularly significant when using order flows from banks, suggesting that banks extract information through trading with other informed traders. Our double-sorted portfolios based on momentum and order flows generate higher returns when the demand for USD hedging is strong.

papers.title: Cross-sectional Momentum in Cryptocurrency Markets
papers.authors: Leigh Drogen, Corey Hoffstein, Kevin Otte
papers.abstract: There is substantial evidence supporting the existence of a short-term momentum anomaly in blockchain based digital assets. Specifically, those assets which perform best (worst) over a 30 day period tend to continue to outperform (underperform) over the subsequent 7 day period. Long-only momentum trading strategies that exploit this phenomenon have consistently delivered excess returns relative to our benchmark (Bitcoin). This paper reviews the evidence of price momentum in cryptocurrency markets, explores the construction of several applicable trading strategies and the potential explanations for the momentum effect.

papers.title: Cross-Sectional Dispersion and the State Dependence of Cryptocurrency Momentum
papers.abstract: This paper studies the state dependence of cross-sectional cryptocurrency momentum in a dynamic, survivorship-aware universe reconstructed from the contemporaneous CoinGecko top 500 with rolling screens for age, market capitalization, trading activity, and return quality. Momentum remains economically meaningful, but lagged cross-sectional dispersion, not generic market volatility, is the variable most closely associated with subsequent breakdown. In horse-race regressions, orthogonalization tests, and asset-level panel specifications, dispersion predicts weaker later momentum returns after controlling for Bitcoin realized volatility and average cross-asset correlation. The effect is nonlinear and concentrated in the upper tail of dispersion, consistent with deterioration in the reliability of the ranking signal. Dispersion-based scaling improves full-sample drawdown and certainty-equivalent outcomes, whereas Bitcoin-volatility scaling performs better in post-2020 long-only implementation exercises. The results distinguish mechanism variables from reduced-form stress proxies and show that inference about cryptocurrency momentum is sensitive to dynamic universe construction.

papers.title: Echo Effect in Cross-Sectional Momentum: Empirical Tests
Macroeconomic Momentum and Cross-Sectional Equity Market
papers.authors: Yu Zhang, Konstantina Kappou, Andrew Urquhart

papers.title: Cross-Sectional Returns in a General Equilibrium: Is There a Momentum?
papers.abstract: The quantitative features of cross-sectional stock returns, such as the momentum and a predictive power of dividend yields on future returns, are not fully understood within a general-equilibrium asset-pricing framework. Especially, the momentum is often considered to be hard to reconcile with the efficient market hypothesis. I calibrate a model with two Lucas trees and the recursive utility. Two trees represent an individual stock (or portfolio) and the rest of the stock market, respectively. The recursive utility is used to provide more realistic predictions on the equity premium and a risk-free rate. The model's predictions on an average individual stock's dividend yield, CAPM and C-CAPM betas, and the gain from a diversification, match reasonably with the data. More importantly, the model is able to generate the momentum profits reported by Lewellen (2002), as well as a cross-sectional regression slope of returns on lagged dividend yields that is close to empirical observations.

papers.title: Causal Momentum: Information Channel Alignment in Network-Based Cross-Sectional Stock Prediction
papers.abstract: We introduce causal momentum (CM), a family of cross-sectional stock features constructed by aggregating the lagged returns of a stock's statistically identified causal drivers within a Granger causality and transfer entropy graph. Applied to an S&P 500 universe of 530 stocks over 2016-2026, CM features achieve a test information coefficient (IC) of 0.203 and an IC information ratio (IR) of 1.42, representing a 14.5% relative improvement over a strong 34-feature fundamental-plus-volatility baseline (IC = 0.177). In contrast, graph neural network (GNN) embeddings trained on the same causal graph degrade predictive performance to an IC of 0.137, a 22.7% deterioration. We propose the information channel alignment hypothesis to explain this result: when a graph encodes return-domain causality, features should remain in the return domain rather than being projected into a latent embedding space. The top-ranked feature by gradient-boosted tree importance is cm_relative-a cross-sectionally normalized measure of the consensus return signal from a stock's causal drivers-which alone captures 4.7% of total model importance. An ablation study across four configurations and a separate six-configuration GNN edge-type analysis confirm that the causal momentum pathway dominates GNN-based alternatives across IC, IC/IR, hit rate, and long-short spread. Our findings challenge the prevailing assumption that graph neural networks are the natural tool for incorporating network structure into quantitative equity models.

papers.title: Macroeconomic Momentum and Cross-Sectional Equity Market Indices
papers.authors: Yu Zhang, Andrew Urquhart, Konstantina Kappou

papers.title: Session Microstructure and the Momentum Mirage: Opening Ranges, Volatility Breakouts, and Cross-sectional Momentum in FX The Deflated Alpha Series
papers.abstract:
Momentum and breakout logic — "price that has recently moved in a direction is more likely to keep
moving in that direction" — is arguably the single most widely taught and traded idea in retail and
institutional FX, and one of the better-documented anomalies in academic finance at longer horizons
and broader instrument universes. This paper subjects four independent operationalizations of that
idea, at four levels of construction sophistication, to the walk-forward, cost-realistic, multiple-testing-
aware protocol developed in Paper 1 of this series, using the four G10 majors (EURUSD, GBPUSD,
AUDUSD, USDJPY) at M5–H4 resolution. Study 1 tests VWAP/EMA-pullback continuation across 12
evaluated combinations and finds two genuine near-misses — USDJPY H1 (+0.266R, permutation p =
0.063) and EURUSD M5 (+0.352R, p = 0.110) — both of which reverse to a negative, closely matched
holdout expectancy (−0.156R and −0.161R) and are reported as inconclusive, not edges. Study 2 tests
opening-range breakout across 4 combinations and finds a clean, decisive negative: all four lose money
out-of-sample and on holdout, with realized win rates falling 5–26 percentage points short of their own
realized breakeven, a shortfall too large in two cases (GBPUSD, AUDUSD) to be explained by costs
alone. Study 3 tests cross-sectional currency momentum across three timeframes and finds a uniformly
negative result that worsens at faster timeframes; it also serves as a worked case study in a generalizable
multi-leg portfolio-accounting pitfall, in which siloed per-leg position sizing against independently
compounding capital bases produced an internally inconsistent combined drawdown reading (−290% of
notional) no real margined account could sustain. Study 4, this paper's methodological centerpiece,
examines two genuinely new volatility-breakout mechanisms across 15 evaluated combinations; four
clear or nearly clear conventional significance (p as low as 0.029), and all four are rejected once the
remainder of this series' validation stack is applied — three of four lose 4–30% of the account on the
untouched holdout, all four show walk-forward efficiency 1.6×–2.9× above this project's acceptable
ceiling (one reading, 4.83, among the most extreme recorded anywhere in this research program), and
the free direction parameter fails to settle on a consistent answer even within a single symbol and
timeframe. We use these four combinations as worked examples of why a single significant p-value is
never sufficient, walking through exactly which of four independent checks — OOS significance, holdout
agreement, walk-forward efficiency, and fold-level direction consistency — catches which failure mode
the others would have missed. Across all four studies, zero combinations clear this series' full validated bar. We argue the comprehensive failure of momentum specifically, set against a series that elsewhere
validates or nearly validates more idiosyncratic structural and behavioral signals (Papers 2–6), is
consistent with momentum being exactly the kind of well-known, heavily arbitraged, textbook-taught
effect that a deep, competitive, continuously electronically intermediated market such as G10 spot FX
should be expected to compete away first.

papers.title: Cross-Sectional Dispersion and the State Dependence of Cryptocurrency Momentum
papers.abstract: This paper studies the state dependence of cross-sectional cryptocurrency momentum in a dynamic, survivorship-aware universe reconstructed from the contemporaneous CoinGecko top 500 with rolling screens for age, market capitalization, trading activity, and return quality. Momentum remains economically meaningful, but lagged cross-sectional dispersion, not generic market volatility, is the variable most closely associated with subsequent breakdown. In horse-race regressions, orthogonalization tests, and asset-level panel specifications, dispersion predicts weaker later momentum returns after controlling for Bitcoin realized volatility and average cross-asset correlation. The effect is nonlinear and concentrated in the upper tail of dispersion, consistent with deterioration in the reliability of the ranking signal. Dispersion-based scaling improves full-sample drawdown and certainty-equivalent outcomes, whereas Bitcoin-volatility scaling performs better in post-2020 long-only implementation exercises. The results distinguish mechanism variables from reduced-form stress proxies and show that inference about cryptocurrency momentum is sensitive to dynamic universe construction.

papers.title: Are Momentum Profits Driven by the Cross-Sectional Dispersion in Expected Stock Returns?
papers.abstract: Consistent with the hypothesis that momentum profits are attributable to the cross-sectional dispersion in expected returns, Bulkley and Nawosah (2009) report that momentum is nonexistent in demeaned returns. Motivated by their work, I examine whether absence of momentum in demeaned returns is robust to methodological adjustments that mitigate microstructure biases. I find that with commonly employed techniques including skipping a month between the formation and holding periods and excluding firms priced less than $5 (penny stocks) from the sample, the mean monthly momentum profit in demeaned returns increases from -0.37% to 1.02% over the 1963 to 2006 sample period. The results highlight the critical importance of using microstructure screens in empirical momentum studies.

papers.title: Cross-Sectional Momentum in Indian Equities: A Reproducible Evaluation on the Nifty-50
The Cost of Sector Constraints in Cross-Sectional Momentum: Evidence from the Nifty 500
papers.abstract: Institutional quantitative equity frameworks routinely mandate sector concentration limits or industry neutrality to eliminate uncompensated macroeconomic sector bets. While developedmarket long-short literature often supports neutralization, recent asset pricing theory [e.g., 6] demonstrates that long-only factor portfolios are systematically impaired by sector constraints because shorting decaying industries is disallowed. We provide an out-of-sample empirical investigation of this hypothesis in the Indian equity market using point-in-time National Stock Exchange (NSE) Nifty 500 constituent data across an 8-year historical sample (January 1, 2018 to February 26, 2026). Evaluating four parametric sector-cap regimes (C ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5}) and one sector-balanced selection regime against an unconstrained benchmark across 10 contiguous out-of-sample evaluation folds (1260 trading days / 5.0 trading years) under realistic transaction costs (42.34 bps round-trip friction including Securities Transaction Tax, stamp duty, exchange levies, and assumed 10 bps execution slippage), we document that all evaluated constrained configurations produce lower realized compound returns and Sharpe ratios than the unconstrained benchmark. An unconstrained 30-stock volatility-adjusted momentum strategy delivers an out-of-sample CAGR of 42.56% and a Sharpe ratio of 1.728. Capping sector allocations to 3 stocks compresses the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) from 0.169 to 0.084, but reduces CAGR to 33.97% (a-8.59pp annual drag) and Sharpe to 1.497 (unadjusted bootstrap p = 0.0204; Holm-adjusted bootstrap p = 0.1020; JKM p = 0.0281), with no improvement in maximum drawdown (-26.79% vs.-26.44%). We find evidence consistent with a factor dilution mechanism: sector caps exclude high-conviction momentum leaders in trending macro sectors, replacing them with lower-ranked securities from lagging industries (average selected momentum rank deteriorates from 15.5 to 48.2), which is positively associated with subsequent relative performance drag in Newey-West HAC predictive regressions (t = 2.41, p = 0.018).

papers.title: Risk-Adjusted Cross-Sectional Momentum
Isolation Forest Anomaly Scores as Incremental Predictors of Cross-Sectional Stock Returns
papers.abstract: We test whether the multi-dimensional unusualness of a firm's fundamental profile, as measured by an Isolation Forest anomaly score, contains incremental information about future stock returns beyond what individual accounting ratios convey when treated as separate predictors. Using annual financial statement data for approximately 4,800 US-listed companies over 2016 to 2024, we construct 18 fundamental features and apply Isolation Forest in a walk-forward design to assign each firm a score that captures how atypical its combination of characteristics is relative to sector peers. This score is then added as an input feature to a LightGBM return prediction model. Comparing the augmented model against a baseline that uses only the 18 fundamental features, we find that the anomaly score adds statistically significant predictive value: the pooled Diebold-Mariano statistic is 2.42 (p = 0.008), and the anomaly score ranks fourth out of 22 features in terms of mean absolute SHAP value. The improvement in out-of-sample R 2 is positive in all four prediction years and robust to variation in the training window, the Isolation Forest contamination parameter, and the sector composition of the sample.

papers.title: Time-Series and Cross-Sectional Momentum in the Saudi Arabia Stock Market Returns
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the presence of time-series and cross-sectional momentum profits and the relationship between these two types of profits in the Saudi Arabia stock market. Results confirm that time-series momentum and cross-sectional contrarian profits are present in this market. The presence of cross-sectional contrarian profits is stronger than that of time-series momentum profits. Cross-sectional contrarian profits are so strong that it remains even after time-series momentum and other market risk factors are considered. An observation period of three months gives the best opportunity to provide cross-sectional contrarian profits. There is a relationship between these two types of momentum profits in the short holding period, but as the holding period increases the relationship fades away.

papers.title: Who dares wins? Cross-sectional momentum and performance rank mobility in China's mutual funds
papers.abstract: This study examines cross-sectional momentum and performance rank mobility in China’s mutual fund market. Using monthly data on equity funds, fixed-income funds, hybrid funds, and fund-of-funds (FOF), we document fund-level momentum with pronounced heterogeneity across categories. Momentum is strongest among equity and hybrid funds, weaker among fixed-income funds, and displays short-horizon reversals for FOFs. Factor-model and instrumental-variable analyses indicate that observed momentum is closely associated with differences in funds’ exposures to equity-level cross-sectional momentum, with the strength of this association varying across market states. Using transition matrices of annual return ranks, we document substantial persistence in relative performance: funds characterised by more active and bolder investment profiles are more likely to move upward or to avoid downward movements in the ranking distribution, with effects that are conditional on market environments. Taken together, the results suggest a systematic interaction between managerial behaviour and market conditions in shaping performance persistence.

papers.title: Hysteresis Rebalancing in Cross-Sectional Momentum: Reducing Boundary Churn and Transaction-Cost Drag in Indian Equities
papers.abstract: In equity markets characterized by double-sided statutory transaction taxation-such as India's Securities Transaction Tax (STT), state stamp duties, and exchange levies-marginal rank turnover at portfolio inclusion boundaries imposes a persistent frictional drag on crosssectional factor strategies. In a conventional monthly momentum strategy selecting the top N = 30 equities, replacing rank N + 1 with rank N incurs two full execution fee legs (≈ 42.34 bps round-trip) to capture a momentum-score differential that is frequently negligible. We formalize and evaluate an asymmetric Hysteresis Rebalancing (Banded) framework on the Indian Nifty 500 universe using point-in-time constituent data from January 2018 through February 2026, with a primary out-of-sample evaluation period from January 2021 through December 2025 (T = 1, 260 contiguous out-of-sample trading days, evaluated over a 10-fold rolling-origin walk-forward protocol). Under this regime, new entrants must achieve a strict top N = 30 momentum rank, whereas incumbent holdings are retained as long as their score remains within an exploratory upper retention buffer (R t (i) ≤ B, for B ∈ {40, 45, 50, 60}). At B = 60, monthly position churn drops by 51.7% (from 9.57 to 4.62 stocks replaced per month), while net after-cost compound annual growth rate (CAGR) improves from 41.70% to 45.12% and the Sharpe ratio rises from 1.728 to 1.849, with maximum drawdown contracting from-26.44% to-25.41%. Although paired stationary bootstrap testing indicates that the after-cost Sharpe gain (∆Sharpe = +0.121, 95% CI [-0.048, +0.310], p = 0.167) is not statistically distinguishable from zero at conventional significance levels, the observed 51.7% reduction in position churn provides evidence that hysteresis banding can materially reduce execution burden in tax-intensive equity markets.

papers.title: Cross-Sectional Momentum in Cryptocurrency: A Net-of-Costs Replication on Tradable Binance Perpetuals (2020-2026)
papers.abstract: Cross-sectional momentum is among the most extensively documented anomalies in asset pricing, and it has been documented in cryptocurrency markets on broad, market-cap-ranked samples. Almost all of that foundational evidence, however, is estimated on data drawn largely from 2014-2020, on universes that include an illiquid tail and are reported gross of trading costs. This note asks a narrower, practitioner-facing question: on a universe of instruments directly tradable by eligible retail participants on Binance USD-Ⓢ M perpetual futures, does a cross-sectional momentum spread remain statistically distinguishable from zero after realistic costs over the more recent 2020-2026 period? Using an independent replication (832 archived perpetual symbols, a daily-close panel, pre-committed J/K parameters, explicit survivorship handling, and three significance tests with different dependence assumptions), we find that neither of the two literaturebacked specifications permitted under a pre-committed protocol (J=1/K=1 and J=2/K=2) yields a net-ofcosts spread distinguishable from zero under any of the three tests. The gross J=1/K=1 spread (+0.573%/week) is of the same order of magnitude as realistic costs (0.40 pp/week) and disappears into noise once they are subtracted; the J=2/K=2 net spread additionally flips sign with an arbitrary choice of rebalancing phase. The contribution is a source-verified synthesis of the existing evidence, an independent net-of-costs test on an actually tradable universe, and a recency check against a literature whose base sample largely predates 2021. We do not claim momentum is a myth: we show that a deliberately constrained, costrealistic implementation on a tradable universe does not translate directly from the academic literature into a tradable retail strategy.

papers.title: The Distribution of Cross Sectional Momentum Returns
papers.authors: Oh Kang Kwon, Stephen E. Satchell

papers.title: From Extinction to Resurrection: Unveiling the Role of Short-Selling Frictions in Cross-Sectional Momentum
papers.abstract: We investigate the impact of short-selling constraints on the cross-sectional momentum effect (CME), unveiling four key findings. First, the CME has nearly vanished after 2000, as short-selling capacity increased. Second, conditioning on short-selling information, the CME remains highly significant for the most constrained stocks. Third, the negative correlation between firm size and momentum, primarily arises from difficulties in short-selling small stocks, especially winners, challenging the "gradual information-diffusion" model. Fourth, we document the predictive role of aggregate sentiment, particularly for losers. These findings support Scheinkman and Xiong (2003)’s prediction of a link between short-selling constraints and asset pricing dynamics.
