papers.title: Advanced Signal Filtering for Mean Reversion trading
papers.authors: Zhichen Xu, Nick Firoozye, Andreas Koukorinis, Philip Treleaven, Wilbur Zhu
papers.abstract: This paper investigates mean reversion trading using advanced neural signal filters. Mean reversion is the assumption that an asset's price will converge to a "fair value", like a simple moving average, over time. The spot asset price, influenced by high-frequency noise, may temporarily be above or below the fair value. Assuming the spot price will revert to the fair price in the long-term, this presents buy or sell opportunities for the reversion trading model. We develop a regime-aware mean-reversion trading framework in which adaptive signal filters determine the latent fair price. We introduce an original optimisation objective; local average filtering objective (LAFO) interpolates between pointwise fitting and global averaging, yielding a controllable low-pass filter. We show how appropriate penalty terms restore identifiability, encode structural regime assumptions, and stabilise the extracted signal. The resulting spot-filter spread and its mean reversion properties can be directly linked to trading performance measures. We further show how modern neural network filters, including recurrent, convolutional, and state-space neural architectures, approximate solutions within this framework.

papers.title: Trading VIX Futures Under Mean Reversion with Regime Switching
Mean Reversion Trading with Sequential Deadlines and Transaction Costs
Mean Reversion in Trading Volume and Informational Efficiency: Evidence from China's Stock Market
Engineering the Mean-Reversion Delay in Dispersion Trading: A Market-Implied Finite-Dimensional Proxy for High-Dimensional Correlation Manifolds
papers.abstract: The dispersion between index and constituent implied volatilities is mathematically equivalent to trading the off-diagonal decay of the return-correlation matrix R_t on the manifold SPD(N) of N×N symmetric positive-definite matrices. The driving economic force is mean reversion of pairwise correlations with latent reversion speed theta = 1/tau, where tau is the mean-reversion delay. Full S&P 500 specification (N=500) faces a double curse of dimensionality: 124,750 free parameters and absent constituent-option liquidity at long tenors. We propose a tractable engineering proxy by (i) projecting onto the MAG7 sub-universe (7×7 matrix, 21 parameters) and (ii) identifying theta non-parametrically from the listed-option term structure via a DTE-mismatch construction. The 15-day gap between index and constituent option tenors yields a market-implied, model-consistent proxy for tau, derived rigorously from a first-passage identification argument on the OU correlation dynamics. We derive the closed-form correlation sensitivity dV/d(rho) under Heston stochastic volatility and provide the complete PnL derivation including second-order Delta-Gamma corrections under tau-compression. A key practical implication is that this construction requires only standard listed options at two expiry dates, placing it within reach of any participant with access to a listed options market — in contrast to variance-swap-based dispersion trades, which require OTC infrastructure unavailable outside institutional settings. The framework converts an intractable stochastic-geometry problem into a theoretically grounded, operationally accessible methodology. All results are theoretical; empirical validation against live market data is necessary before any practical conclusions can be drawn.

papers.title: Analysis of the Bollinger bands and Ornstein-Uhlebeck Model Mean Reversion Trading Strategy in S&P 500 Equities
Peer Group Beta Reliability under Thin Trading Conditions: Results from a Simulated Environment in the Standard, Mean-Reversion and, Bayesian Framework.
papers.abstract: Finance literature has proposed numerous techniques in order to eradicate the effects of thin trading, ranging from (il-)liquidity indicators indicating distortions in beta estimates to beta correction procedures directly correcting them in the traditional market model. This study exam-ines the superiority of comprehensive sets of 16 popular (il-)liquidity indicators and 10 popular beta correction procedures among themselves as well as against each other according to bias (effi-ciency) and accuracy (predictive ability) in the standard framework. Furthermore, the analysis is duplicated for the mean-reversion and the Bayesian framework, thus relaxing the assumption of beta stationarity. The results indicate (i) the (il-)liquidity indicators to generally outperform the beta correction procedures in small as well as in large stock markets, across different levels of thin trad-ing, across different levels of risk (beta magnitudes) and, across all three market model frame-works, (ii) the Illiquidity (Amihud-Hasbrouck) Indicator and the Return-to-Turnover Indicator as well as the Trade-to-Trade Method to dominate in the standard and the mean-reversion frame-work, (iii) the Turnover Indicator as well as the Error Correction Model to dominate in the Bayesian framework and, (iv) the (il-)liquidity indicators to generate absolutely best indications on beta dis-tortions in the Bayesian framework as well as the beta correction procedures to generate absolute-ly best beta estimates in the standard framework.

papers.title: Optimal Pairs Trading: A Mean-Variance Approach Incorporating a Stop-Loss Mechanism
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the optimal pairs trading problem within a continuous-time mean-variance (MV) framework. The spread between two risky assets is modeled as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process. To mitigate potential losses arising from a non-converging spread, we incorporate a stop-loss mechanism. Owing to the time inconsistency of the mean-variance criterion, we derive an explicit equilibrium strategy by solving the extended Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation. Furthermore, we conduct numerical experiments to illustrate the equilibrium strategy and assess its performance.

papers.title: Optimal Dynamic Pairs Trading of Futures Under a Two-Factor Mean-Reverting Model
Optimal Pairs Trading Strategies: a Stochastic Mean-Variance Approach
papers.authors: Fenghui Yu, Wai-Ki Ching, Chufang WU, Jiawen Gu

papers.title: Time-Consistent Mean-Variance Pairs-Trading Under Regime-Switching Cointegration
papers.authors: Kexin Chen, Mei Choi Chiu, Hoi Ying Wong

papers.title: Mean Reversion Indexing
papers.abstract: In their 1985 paper ‘Does the stock market overeact?', DeBondt and Thaler explained the idea of mean reversion and how it leads to the Loser’s portfolio of 3 years outperforming the Winner’s portfolio of the same time. Based on mean reversion, this paper illustrates a new stock selection and trend determining approach. The paper uses an innovative approach to convert price performance data into non price ranking data, which is positively tested for mean reversion and stationarity.

papers.title: Super Mean Reversion
papers.abstract: Mean reversion processes are classified as either partially, fully, or super mean reverting. The term super mean reversion is reserved here for the case where the reversal is particularly strong and larger in magnitude than the original shock. Among the three types of mean reversion, super mean reversion is certainly the more obscure. However, it is not contradictory in any way to the stability requirements of time series analysis (stationarity and ergodicity). Rarity of empirical findings may be attributed to the rarity of super mean reversion in the real world, to the possible discarding of such results as unreliable, or to the use of incorrect tests. This paper argues that the variance ratio test is unsuitable for detection of super mean reversion. Constrained autoregressive tests may be more suitable for this purpose.

papers.title: Optimal Pairs Trading with Dynamic Mean-Variance
papers.authors: Dongmei ZHU, Jia-Wen Gu, Feng-Hui Yu, Tak-Kuen Siu, Wai-Ki Ching

papers.title: Competitive Equilibrium and Mean Reversion
papers.abstract: A competitive equilibrium stock price or ETF price on the market portfolio supports the efficient markets hypothesis. Other studies reject the efficient markets hypothesis. An adapted CIR theory models mean reversion in stock prices with uncorrelated stock returns. Previous leading models of mean reversion with mean-reverting errors induce negative serially correlated multi-period stock returns. This result seemingly violates market efficiency. Mean reversion is modeled as the outcome of the adjustment of stock prices to news. A model of a competitive equilibrium stock price explains stock price behavior involving corporate activities which change the supply of common stocks.

papers.title: Considerations on the mean-reversion time
Markov and the Mean Reversion Framework
papers.abstract: Natural systems witness reversion and divergence simultaneously across different periods of time. This paper tests the performance proxy as mentioned in a previous paper on the ‘Mean Reversion Framework’ for Markov’s transition probabilities. The framework exhibits a stable pattern when tested for STOXX 50, S&P 100, Nikkei 225 and FTSE 100 components across different periods of time from 20 days to 3750 days. The three bin classifications of the framework; value, growth and core exhibit a consistency in growth and decay pattern. Both value and growth exhibit persistence compared to the core bin and tends to decay slowly. While the core bins show a symmetric decay across other bins. Such a probabilistic behavior in group components leads the author to believe that the mean reversion framework is indeed converging and diverging leading to a robust expression of a stock market system. The framework could work across data sets from various domains, confirming the proposed universality of the mean reversion framework.

papers.title: Mean Reversion: A New Approach
papers.abstract: In this paper, we review briefly existing approaches to statistical arbitrage and mean reversion and then proceed to present a new approach that combines model-independence, through the use of neural networks, with information theory. The neural networks parameters were calibrated in a way that guarantees mean reversion, using a loss function that aims to maximise the entropy of the power spectrum of the error instead of the traditionally minimised mean squared error. The returns of a signal-based strategy derived from this new approach were empirically illustrated using historical stocks data from several US firms. The results showed significant gains can be realised by using this new approach.

papers.title: Expectations of Profitability Mean-Reversion in Europe
papers.abstract: We have found that for net income and earnings before interest and tax the average expected rate of profitability mean reversion (exactly rate of abnormal profitability deterioration) differs significantly from approx. 10 % to 80 % (depending on the estimation method used). Overally results can be understood also that way that investors are rather optimists, expecting the badly performing companies to regain their profitability and the well-performing to keep their superior profitability. Averages of subsequent ROE and ROIC mean-reversion indicate that investors are not far from true.

papers.title: Cash Flow Certainty And Intraday Mean-Reversion Reliability
papers.abstract: We present empirical evidence that the reliability of intraday mean reversion in U.S. Equity prices is strongly predicted by the certainty of the underlying company's cash flows. Using a systematic trading framework combining Time Segmented Volume (TSV) regime filtering with an exponential moving average fair value (FV) anchor, we test a single unoptimized parameter set across 22 liquid stocks spanning five sectors over 150 trading days (August 2025-March 2026). Energy midstream/infrastructure stocks, characterized by contracted, predictable cash flows, exhibit consistent mean-reversion behavior with risk-adjusted returns (Sharpe ratios 3.2-10.6) significantly exceeding those of consumer staples stocks with competitive, uncertain cash flows (Sharpe ratios-3.6 to 0.7). The finding is robust to the use of fixed parameters across stocks within a sector, eliminating curve-fitting concerns. We propose that institutional response to price dislocations is mediated by cash flow visibility: when future revenues are contractually secured, informed buyers treat price declines as temporary dislocations and act quickly, producing reliable mean reversion detectable via volume flow analysis. When cash flows are competitively determined, the same price declines may represent fundamental repricing, producing sustained directional moves that defeat mean-reversion strategies.

papers.title: An Extended Mean-Reversion Test for Relative Stock Prices
papers.abstract: Recent tests of mean reversion in relative stock prices do not acknowledge the fact that relative stock prices can be drifting due to, for example, different risk characteristics of the underlying stock portfolios. Consequently, they impose the wrong form of stationarity. We propose a test for mean reversion in relative stock prices based on the integration of a restricted trend stationarity tests and constrained autoregressive tests. The unified test is superior to the current methodology in two respects. First, it employs the correct form of stationarity. Second, it allows for both partial and full mean reversion of the price differential rather than the currently used restrictive assumption of full mean reversion.

papers.title: Closed-End Fund Abnormal Returns and Discount Mean-Reversion
papers.abstract: Swedish investment companies structured as closed-end funds (CEFs) are large relative to CEFs in the U.S. and elsewhere. Their costs are low and they trade at high and mean-revering discounts. I show that CEF returns are usually in excess of what can be explained by conventional risk factors. I decompose returns into return on CEF assets, return due to leverage, return due to changes in discount and other (abnormal) return. The latter is significantly positive for a portfolio of CEFs. This is exploited in a trading strategy which delivers abnormal returns of more than 10% annually. The CEFs are in essence conglomerates with listed holdings. This makes it possible to disentangle different reasons for the conglomerate discount. Discounts cannot be (fully) explained by inefficiencies, costs and potential agent problems. This suggests that investors do demand a discount for investing in a portfolio they cannot chose themselves.

papers.title: Statistical Modeling and Trading Strategies: The Case of Pairs Trading
papers.abstract: Advance in time series analysis has enabled us to examine various economic phenomena for descriptive purposes, but does it translate to trading profits? Using pairs trading as a testing ground, this paper finds that strategies that are formulated around stationary pricing relations using autoregressive and cointegration models are better able to identify predictable pricing relations compared to simple non-parametric methods. However, the mispricings that are picked up by these time series models are smaller in magnitude compared to the non-parametric counterpart. Overall, strategies using statistical modelling do not generate greater pairs trading profits.

papers.title: Using Trend-Following Managed Futures to Increase Expected Withdrawal Rates
papers.abstract: Decreased bond yields substantially increase the probability of portfolio depletion for investors using an initial 4% withdrawal rate. One way to increase the safe withdrawal rate of a portfolio is alter the composition of the portfolio without changing the portfolio’s overall risk level. I propose a portfolio construction solution that incorporates trend-following managed futures into portfolios. The resulting portfolio, consisting of 50% stocks, 40% bonds and 10% trend-following managed futures, allows an investor to increase “safe” initial withdrawal rates while still maintaining a similar risk profile to a traditional 50% stock and 50% bond portfolio.

papers.title: Commodity Futures Trading Strategies: Trend-Following and Calendar Spreads
papers.abstract: This brief article discusses the most common strategies employed by futures traders, namely: trend-following and calendar-spread trading.

papers.title: Has Machine Learning Defeated Trend Following Strategies in the Chinese Futures Market
papers.abstract: This study investigates the comparative performance of machine learning methods versus traditional trend-following strategies in predicting returns in the Chinese commodity futures market from 2015 to 2023. Utilizing transaction data from major Chinese futures exchanges, we applied various machine learning models including Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), Transformer Encoder, Decision Tree, XGBoost, and LightGBM. These were contrasted with traditional methods such as Rate of Change, Moving Averages, and On Balance Volume. Our findings indicate that machine learning models, particularly MLP, significantly outperformed traditional strategies, achieving higher annualized excess returns and Sharpe ratios. Machine learning's ability to capture complex patterns and leverage both volume and price data proved crucial, especially in managing higher frequency trading that incurs significant transaction costs. By setting a neutral probability threshold for trading signals, we further analyzed the strategic advantages of machine learning in optimizing trade timing and profitability. These results suggest that machine learning can offer substantial benefits over traditional approaches, especially in volatile and liquid markets like those of Chinese commodities.

papers.title: Evaluating Interpretable Meta-Labeling for Intraday Futures Trend Following: Open-Interest Features and Contract-Dependent Outcomes
papers.authors: Bing Zhang, Zhiwen Chang, Yu Zhang, Junqing Wang
papers.abstract: This study evaluates an interpretable meta-labeling framework for intraday futures trend following, in which a deterministic moving-average rule generates candidate crossover events and an XGBoost secondary classifier filters them. The evaluation uses 15-minute data from five Chinese futures contracts spanning commodity and equity-index markets. Six z-scored predictors describe the local state; one predictor is the bar-level percentage change in open interest. Triple-barrier labels (TP=1.0%, SL=0.6%, H=60) drive a five-fold purged walk-forward out-of-sample evaluation with primary seed-42 and a pre-specified robustness seed-2024, under a pre-specified aggregate 4-bps round-trip cost assumption. Shared-target ROC-AUC values cluster near 0.5 across contracts and classifiers, indicating weak rank-order discrimination between TP-labeled and non-TP-labeled candidate events. Under the primary seed, the Meta-XGB event-level Ret/MDD difference versus Raw-MA is positive for C and IC and negative for RB, AU and TA. None of the five paired stationary-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals at expected block length ℓ = 20 excludes zero. Under the pre-specified robustness seed, RB and TA retain negative point-estimate signs and C retains a positive sign, while AU and IC change sign; no paired 95% interval excludes zero under either seed. At τ = 0.50, Meta-XGB accepts only 1.44%-6.76% of candidate events. SHAP attribution identifies which predictors the fitted model uses, and ablation tests incremental economic contribution. Open-interest changes are influential model inputs in several contracts, but their incremental economic contribution is contract-dependent and not uniformly positive. The evidence supports meta-labeling as an interpretable contract-dependent decision-support layer rather than as a universally performance-improving filter.

papers.title: Trend Following, Risk Parity and Momentum in Commodity Futures
papers.authors: Steve H. Thomas, Andrew D. Clare, James Seaton, Peter N. Smith

papers.title: Designing Robust Trend-following System: Behind the Scenes of Trend-following
papers.abstract:
Trend-following has actively been on investors’ radar for the last few decades. The J.P. Morgan primer on momentum strategies (Kolanovic and Wei, 2015) provides an extensive review of the momentum strategies. The current paper focuses on a concrete trend-following solution and analyzes its properties alongside the practical implementation.
More concretely, the goal of the current paper is threefold:

• First, a trend-following signal based on statistical theory is proposed and we analytically investigate its properties. We reconcile the theoretical results with stylized facts about trend-following investing – ‘CTA smile’, the link to straddles and the better performance of so-called ‘slower’ signals.

• Second, based on the theoretical results we propose a prototype trend-following solution that uses a unified approach across assets and diversifies across time-frames. Its performance versus benchmarks and diversification properties for long-only portfolios are highlighted within simulation examples.

• Third, we elaborate on the portfolio and risk management of the trend-following strategy. We illustrate how the risk-budgeting and the Hierarchical Risk Parity (HRP) approaches can be adapted to the trend-following framework. Various methods to manage the transaction costs aspects of the strategy have also been discussed. In particular, we show how to limit the downside in the case of trendless market and how to take into account the implications of the carry component in many futures and FX forwards.

papers.title: Alpha on Trend-Following Beta: a case study of the SocGen Trend Index
papers.abstract: Trend strategies have long been praised for their appealing qualities as effective means of portfolio diversification, and for other attractive features that have been thoroughly documented in the literature, such as low correlation with equity markets bringing protection from drawdowns. Indexes such as the BarclayHedge BTOP50 Index and the Société Générale SG Trend Index track the performance of a basket of funds dedicated to trend-following and managed futures strategies (CTAs). However, misspecification and poor execution of a trend-following strategy can lead to severe risks. Building on the concepts from [Braun et al., 2024] and [Hurst et al., 2013], we expand the above work on replication of trend-following strategies in CTAs while substantially reducing the number of assets (hence the turnover) and diversifying in replication methodology, achieving a superior performance in terms of Sharpe ratio. We take as benchmark the SG Trend Index.

papers.title: Optimal Trend Following Portfolios
papers.abstract: This paper derives an optimal portfolio that is based on trend-following signal. Building on an earlier related article, it provides a unifying theoretical setting to introduce an autocorrelation model with the covariance matrix of trends and risk premia. We specify practically relevant models for the covariance matrix of trends. The optimal portfolio is decomposed into four basic components that yield four basic portfolios: Markowitz, risk parity, agnostic risk parity, and trend following on risk parity. The overperformance of the proposed optimal portfolio, applied to cross-asset trading universe, is confirmed by empirical backtests. We provide thus a unifying framework to describe and rationalize earlier developed portfolios.

papers.title: Diversification and Convexity in Trend Following
papers.abstract: How does the cross-sectional filter of a trend-following portfolio determine its Sharpe ratio and its convexity, and can a filter raise the first without giving up the second? In a Gaussian benchmark, the return of any filter is a weighted sum of independent single-market trend followers, weighted by the eigenvalues of the filter times the correlation matrix. For the classic equal-risk portfolio, convexity breadth never exceeds Sharpe breadth: 73 futures markets offer about fifteen independent Sharpe bets but only four convexity bets, and skewness stops falling at about 16 markets. Targeting the volatility of current positions removes most of the remaining convexity. The Sharpe-optimal filter weights directions by trend premium and earns lead-lag premia. Estimated by a risk-premium PCA, it raises the walk-forward Sharpe ratio from 0.60 to 1.33 with no detectable loss of convexity; net of costs, it nearly matches a volatility-targeted reference system but keeps the skewness that the target removes.

papers.title: A New Approach To Trend-Following
papers.abstract: Investment professionals, and some academics, have long believed that asset prices tend to move in trends. Practitioners have attempted to profit from this belief by buying assets with positive trends and selling assets with negative trends. Many studies document the historical outperformance of trend-following strategies relative to their buy-and-hold counterparts. However, trend-following's reported profitability is likely to be overstated. Moreover, typical implementations of trend-following strategies have multiple undesirable properties. The goal of this paper is to identify the strengths and weaknesses of common trend-following strategies and develop a way to emphasize the strengths while minimizing or eliminating the weaknesses. First, I review the literature and assess the viability of trend-following strategies. After concluding that a multi-asset trend-following strategy can in fact add value when higher moments are considered, I propose an improved trend-following strategy that considers distances between assets and downside risk via a hierarchical clustering algorithm. Finally, I show that merging machine learning techniques with a simple trend-following rule consistently outperforms a traditional risk parity approach with lower turnover, especially in recent periods.

papers.title: Power Assisted Trend Following
papers.abstract: “The trend is your friend” is a common saying, the difficulty lies in determining if and when you are in a trend. Is the trend strong enough to trade? When does the trend reverse and how are you going to determine this? We will try and answer at least some of these questions here. We are deriving a novel indicator to measure the power of a trend using digital signal processing techniques, separating the Signal from the Noise. We apply these to examples as well as real data and evaluate the accuracy of these and the relation to P&L performance of the "Volatility Index" trend following algorithm devised by J. Welles Wilder Jr. in 1978.

papers.title: Rethinking Trend Following: Optimal Regime-Dependent Allocation
papers.abstract: We propose a simple and transparent theoretical framework for optimal regime-dependent allocation in trend-following strategies. While the existing literature on time-series momentum and related approaches focuses primarily on signal construction, portfolio exposures are typically imposed exogenously. In contrast, we treat detected market regimes as conditioning information and derive regime-specific asset exposures directly from a Sharpe-ratio maximization problem. The resulting allocation rule is fully tractable, applies to an arbitrary number of market regimes, and nests standard trend-following strategies as special, and generally suboptimal, cases. Using U.S. equity portfolios, international equity indices, and a broad set of diversified portfolio datasets, we show that optimal regime-dependent allocation delivers economically meaningful and robust improvements in out-of-sample risk-adjusted performance relative to the time-series momentum strategy of Moskowitz, Ooi, and Pedersen (2012) and the dynamic speed momentum strategy of Goulding, Harvey, and Mazzoleni (2023). These gains persist across assets and portfolio implementations, highlighting the central role of optimal positioning in trend following.

papers.title: Trend Following System for Stock Index Trading
papers.abstract: There have been wide applications of trend following based trading system in the real world. The traditional methods include 5 days moving average, 20 days moving average, 200 days moving average and so on. If the midterm market trend is the biggest concern, 20 days and 50 days moving averages can provide efficient forecast information about stock trend. However, the solo stock price moving average does not provide sentimental information of the market in a timely manner. This paper discusses a mathematical formulation of stock trend decision and the related prediction delay problem. An efficient method which utilizes the market sentiment Index has been proposed, aiming to forecast short term and long term market tops and bottoms. This new method leads to specific trading rules on two major indexes SPY and QQQQ. The experimental results show very accurate position estimation and support that our system implements much more reliable trading rules than the bench mark buy and hold strategy in terms of market exposure and account balance.

papers.title: Some Observations on Trend Following: A Binomial Perspective
papers.abstract: This paper uses a simple binomial framework to explore trend following. It shows (by counter example) that the existence of positive profits from trend-following strategies, on its own, provides no prima facie evidence on the efficiency or inefficiency of markets. In addition, it explores the most important feature of time series momentum investment strategies: the return shaping impact of trend following through its dynamic positioning. In a stylized efficient market setting (with no transaction costs), the paper shows that the dynamic nature of trend following shapes when profits and losses occur compared to a buy-and-hold strategy. There is, however, a conservation of “mass” in that gains and losses are shuffled across periods such that the unconditional distribution of profits is unaffected. In this sense, trend following, by construction, generates crisis alpha --- for crises where large losses occur over extended periods of time. Due to its ability to shape when profit and losses occur, trend following can provide significant portfolio diversification and hedging potential for those investors with strategic risk-on exposures.

papers.title: Trend-following Strategies for Crypto Investors
papers.abstract: In the rapidly evolving landscape of financial markets, the emergence of cryptocurrencies as a distinct asset class has opened up new avenues for investors. However, investors need to establish a comprehensive investment strategy and implement risk-management measures before entering this space to mitigate the potential for market crashes. This paper develops and evaluates trendfollowing investment strategies in the context of cryptocurrencies. Secondly, it investigates the commonly held belief of a correlation between the movements of the Nasdaq 100 index and cryptocurrencies, which has significant implications for investment strategy development. We find that trend following strategies perform well over the researched period. Moreover, the effect of transaction costs is very substantial on portfolio performances. We also find no correlation between Nasdaq 100 index and our investigated cryptos, inconsistent with common perception in the market.

papers.title: The Effective Win Rate of Trend-Following Strategies
papers.abstract: I provide a method for estimating the effective win rate of trend-following strategies so that fair comparisons can be made with higher-frequency methods. As trend-following strategies make money from outlier trades with long holding periods, changing the average holding period based on hypothetical rebalancing results in a higher effective win rate than what is measured by the fraction of winning trades.

papers.title: Echoing Messages: Narrative Trend-Following and Transient Capital
papers.abstract: When managers tilt their earnings-call narratives toward the themes analysts have recently been probing, short-horizon mutual funds increase their positions while moderate-and longhorizon funds do not. The effect is amplified among firms where independent verification of narrative content is costly and intensifies after the mid-2010s diffusion of open-source Natural language processing (NLP) tools, concentrating in the machine-readable components of alignment. Value-weighted portfolios formed on alignment earn negative Fama-French fivefactor alpha over the four months following formation, and high-alignment firms subsequently miss earnings forecasts and experience margin erosion despite continued revenue growth. The horizon gradient in trading, the concentration in opaque firms, and the divergence between revenue growth and profitability jointly weigh against a signaling interpretation and support a catering channel in which narrative conformity attracts transient capital that is repriced once hard information arrives.

papers.title: A Guide to Trend Following Strategies
papers.abstract:
Trend following is one of the most popular and enduring systematic trading strategies. An attractive long-term track record and strong returns during market crises have resulted in trend following becoming a vital component in many portfolios.

In this paper we analyze the general profile of trend following strategies, and demonstrate how to build such a strategy in four steps.

papers.title: Trend Following Strategies: A Practical Guide
The Science and Practice of Trend-following Systems
papers.abstract:
We present a unified approach to designing trend-following (TF) systems and classify them into European, American, and Time Series Momentum categories. For European TF systems, we derive an exact relationship between profit-and-loss, autocorrelation, and drift in volatility-normalized returns. We analyze the expected return under fractional ARFIMA processes and show that TF systems are profitable when the long-term autocorrelation is positive, even under short-term mean reversion. In the frequency domain, the expected return is represented as a Poisson-kernel reading of the analytical or empirical spectrum of the volatility-normalized returns: the system profits at zero drift when the kernel-weighted spectral mass exceeds one, so trend-following alpha is excess spectral mass at low frequencies. Longer lookbacks benefit in addition from the squared drift of the return process. We derive the closed-form Sharpe ratio, with the excess kurtosis of the innovations entering through a single loading, and the net Sharpe ratio and cost-optimal span under trading costs. Under white noise, we derive the closed-form skewness of aggregated TF returns, which is positive at every horizon and peaks near half the filter span. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the analytical results. We show that the positive skewness of TF returns is structural under various model assumptions. Empirically, we evaluate the systems on liquid contracts, and show that all TF systems are strongly correlated and our analytical results can be applied for their performance attribution. Our results enable design, simulation, and performance attribution of TF systems from trend persistence, mean reversion, drift, and skewness.
This is joint work with Vladimir Lucic.

papers.title: A Trend Factor in Commodity Futures Markets: Any Economic Gains From Using Information Over Investment Horizons?
papers.abstract: This paper identifies a trend factor that exploits the short-, intermediate-, and long-run moving averages of settlement prices in commodity futures markets. The trend factor generates statistically and economically large returns during the post-financialization period 2004-2020. It outperforms the well-known momentum factor by more than nine times the Sharpe ratio and has less downside risk. The trend factor cannot be explained by the existing factor models and is priced cross-sectionally. Finally, we find that the trend factor is correlated with funding liquidity measured by the TED spread. Overall, the results indicate that there are significant economic gains from using the information on historical prices in commodity futures markets.

papers.title: Trend: Catch Me If You Can! A Business Case for MNTO: A Quantitative Proprietary Trading Model Long Only Trend Following Strategy
papers.abstract: MNTO is an actively-managed investment vehicle based on a statistically validated proprietary trading model. Its combined approach integrates financial engineering, trading psychology, market adaptability and money management, and aims to generate superior returns with excellent risk-reward properties and a low correlation to directional market movements. The results of 4 years of research on this long-only trend-following strategy are based on the ASX50 stocks and the historical ex-post examination spans over 11 years [2000-2010] incorporating 10 years of backtesting and 1 year of paper trading. Transaction costs (inclusive of slippage, commission, and market impact), overnight gaps and liquidity were accounted for, and tests for survivorship bias were also conducted. The empirical results strongly suggest that the Quantitative Proprietary Trading Model – Long-Only Trend-Following Strategy – has a competitive advantage in being a profitable trading system and earning sound risk adjusted excess returns.

papers.title: Increasing Diversification of Commodities Trend-Following Strategies
The Trend is Our Friend: Risk Parity, Momentum and Trend Following in Global Asset Allocation
papers.authors: Andrew D. Clare, Peter N. Smith, Stephen H. Thomas
papers.abstract: We examine the effectiveness of applying a trend following methodology to global asset allocation between equities, bonds, commodities and real estate. The application of trend following offers a substantial improvement in risk-adjusted performance compared to traditional buy-and-hold portfolios. We also find it to be a superior method of asset allocation than risk parity. Momentum and trend following have often been used interchangeably although the former is a relative concept and the latter absolute. By combining the two we find that one can achieve the higher return levels associated with momentum portfolios but with much reduced volatility and drawdowns due to trend following. We observe that a flexible asset allocation strategy that allocates capital to the best performing instruments irrespective of asset class enhances this further.

papers.title: Kalman Innovations as a Credibility Check for Trend-Following Signals
papers.abstract: Moving-average crossovers are a standard trend-following signal. But on a broad panel of roughly 1,100 stocks, more than half of their reversal signals do not correspond to a DC-defined reversal. Kalman's innovation term — the discrepancy between a filter's prediction and the observed price, a direct measure of how surprising that observation was — offers an orthogonal check. In engineering, it has served as an established diagnostic since the 1970s, used in fields from navigation to fault detection; in finance, it has not yet received the attention it deserves. We demonstrate that this signal separates DC-defined reversals from the short-lived whipsaws long familiar from moving-average crossover systems, both on this broad panel and on an independently constructed, curated panel of 101 stocks. The effect uses only information available at the signal date.

papers.title: The Trend is Our Friend: Risk Parity, Momentum and Trend Following in Global Asset Allocation
papers.authors: Andrew D. Clare, James Seaton, Peter N. Smith, Stephen H. Thomas
papers.abstract: We examine the effectiveness of applying a trend following methodology to global asset allocation between equities, bonds, commodities and real estate. The application of trend following offers a substantial improvement in risk-adjusted performance compared to traditional buy-and-hold portfolios. We also find it to be a superior method of asset allocation than risk parity. We believe the discipline of trend following overcomes many of the behavioural biases investors succumb to, such as regret and herding. The other side of behavioural biases is that they may be exploited by investors: the clearest example of this is momentum investing where herding leads to continuation of returns and has been identified across many asset classes. Also, momentum and trend following have often been used interchangeably although the former is a relative concept and the latter absolute. By combining the two we find that one can achieve the higher return levels associated with momentum portfolios but with much reduced volatility and drawdowns due to trend following. We compare the performance of selected strategies using measures based on the utility function of a representative investor. These results reinforce the superiority of combining trend following with momentum strategies. We observe that a flexible asset allocation strategy that allocates capital to the best performing instruments irrespective of asset class enhances this further.

papers.title: Evaluating the Performance of Systematic Trend-Following and Global Macro Strategies
papers.abstract: This study conducts a detailed exploration of two prominent investment strategies: systematic trend-following and systematic global macro. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset encompassing diverse countries, asset classes, and economic indicators, we evaluate the performance of these strategies both independently and in combination. A key innovation in our systematic trend-following approach involves incorporating the magnitude of price movements, alongside their direction, significantly enhancing strategy performance. In the realm of global macro strategies, we delve into the intricate relationship between macroeconomic variables and market dynamics, uncovering insights into asset price determinants. When these strategies are integrated, they not only complement each other’s strengths but also demonstrate a remarkable synergy. This amalgamation yields a diversified portfolio approach with minimal correlation to the equity market, thereby offering a potent tool for risk mit- igation and portfolio diversification. Overall, our findings illuminate the nuanced intricacies of these strategies and their potential to redefine portfolio management paradigms.

papers.title: Can the Variability of Trend-Following Signals Add Value?
Does Trend-Following Still Work on Stocks?
papers.authors: Carlo Zarattini, Alberto Pagani, Cole Wilcox

papers.title: Regime Sequencing in Trend Following Systems: Evidence from Four Developed Equity Markets
papers.abstract: This paper tests whether sequencing, the order in which a trend following tool and a mean reversion oscillator are permitted to act relative to a market regime classification, materially affects risk adjusted performance. Using a 63 trading day rolling linear regression R squared to classify daily regime state, and a 5,3 Stochastic oscillator conditioned on that classification, we test four rule variants against a buy and hold benchmark across four developed equity indices: the S&P 500 (United States, 2000 to 2025), the FTSE 100 (United Kingdom, 2013 to 2023), the DAX (Germany, 2013 to 2023), and the Nikkei 225 (Japan, 2000 to 2020). We find that conditioning the oscillator to act only once a trend is already confirmed by the regression, rather than during unconfirmed or ranging periods, produces higher Sharpe and Calmar ratios than an unconditioned trend following benchmark in three of the four markets, and dramatically outperforms buy and hold in the one market that exhibited multi decade directional stagnation over the sample period. We further test three risk overlays, a fixed percentage stop, volatility scaled position sizing, and a monthly reset stop, and find that volatility scaled sizing consistently produces the best risk adjusted outcome while a fixed percentage stop typically produces the highest absolute return. All rules tested are fully mechanical and require no discretionary judgment to apply. We report full parameter values, data sources, and limitations, and note that these findings do not extend to at least one emerging market index tested outside this paper's developed market scope, where the underlying index drift was strong enough that no active variant outperformed simple buy and hold.

papers.title: Optimal Trend Following Trading Rules
papers.authors: Min Dai, Zhou Yang, Qing Zhang, Qiji Jim Zhu
papers.abstract: This paper is concerned with the optimality of a trend following trading rule. The idea is to catch a bull market at its early stage, ride the trend, and liquidate the position at the first evidence of the subsequent bear market. We characterize the bull and bear phases of the markets mathematically using the conditional probabilities of the bull market given the up to date stock prices. The optimal buying and selling times are given in terms of a sequence of stopping times determined by two threshold curves. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the theoretical results and demonstrate how they perform in a marketplace.

papers.title: Tuning Trend Following Strategies with Macro ESG Data
papers.authors: Christian Morgenstern, Guillaume Coqueret, James Kelly
papers.abstract: Trend Following (TF) is a well-known and documented strategy which has been employed by practitioners since the 1980s. The focus so far has been on the alpha-generating potential of the strategies and in particular on extending the strategy to a broader range of asset markets. In this paper, we describe how to integrate sovereign Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) information into a macro TF strategy. Notably, we find that the ESG exposure of the macro portfolios can be substantially increased without any cost in performance.

papers.title: Carry Trade, Forward Premium Puzzle and Currency Crisis
papers.abstract: Recent many empirical studies have argued that currency carry trade have been a driving force behind exchange rate movements, and have explained the latest financial crisis of 2007-2009 in terms of a sudden, massive reversal of carry trade positions. The aim of this paper is to provide one potential theoretical explanation for questions why currency carry trade becomes profitable, and why a sudden unwinding of carry trade is caused. We propose a new behavioral model of currency bubbles and crashes. We consider that investors trade two currencies: the domestic currency, and the foreign currency. Investors are divided into two groups, the rational investors and the carry traders. The rational investors maximize their expected utility of their wealth in the next period. Carry traders maximize their random utility of binary choice: investing the domestic currency or investing the foreign currency. We demonstrate that carry-traders’ herd behavior, which follows the behavior getting a majority, gives cause to a currency bubble, and their carry trading prolongs bubble. However, depreciation of funding currency slows down as the carry-trader’s behavior approaches to a stationary state, so that the return on carry trade predicted by carry traders begins to decrease in the second half of bubble. We demonstrate that decreasing the return on carry trade predicted by carry traders lead to currency crash. Our model also gives a plausible explanation on the forward premium puzzle.

papers.title: Currency Carry Trade and Bank's Foreign Exchange Risk Management
papers.abstract: The role of the market makers is crucial in determining the foreign exchange risk premium in currency carry trade. A typical market maker of foreign exchange is a highly leveraged commercial bank or investment bank. I derive a model of foreign exchange risk premium from the perspective of a market maker, in which the required foreign exchange risk premium is proportional to the volatility of foreign exchange rate, the net foreign exchange exposure, and the financial leverage. The financial leverage amplifies small changes in net foreign exposure and volatility into large changes in the risk premium. This amplifier effect offers an explanation to the foreign exchange risk premium puzzle. I use this model to examine the negative interest rate differential between Japan and the U.S. in the 1990s.

papers.title: Carry Trade and Currency Crash Risk
papers.abstract: This paper examines the role of currency crash risk in explaining the persistent profitability of carry trades. Focusing on the US Dollar–Turkish Lira market, we construct three forward-looking measures of crash risk: risk reversals, crash probabilities from option-implied distributions, and jump risk from a jump-diffusion model. Using survey-based exchange rate expectations, we separate ex ante carry premia from ex post surprises. Our results show that higher crash risk significantly increases expected returns, indicating that investors demand compensation for bearing such risk rather than arbitraging away mispricing. Shapley decomposition attributes over 20\% of the explained variance in expected carry returns to crash risk, while balance sheet constraints and global risk aversion further reinforce premia. A comparison of hedged and unhedged strategies reveals that 46–77\% of carry returns reflect compensation for crash exposure.

papers.title: The Currency Carry Trade
Flow Tomography: Pseudoinverse Decomposition of Currency Flows from Pair-Level Returns with Application to Cross-Currency Contagion and Carry Trade Dissolution
papers.abstract: This paper develops and empirically tests a pseudoinverse-based method for decomposing observable currency pair returns into latent individual currency flows. Each currency pair return is a linear projection of two underlying currency flows; with 12 pairs spanning 8 currencies, the system is overdetermined and solvable by least squares. The composition matrix C maps currency

papers.title: Currency Momentum, Carry Trade, and Market Illiquidity
Currency Regimes and the Carry Trade
papers.authors: Olivier Accominotti, Jason Cen, David Chambers, Ian William Marsh
papers.abstract: This study exploits a new long-run data set of daily bid and offered exchange rates in spot and forward markets from 1919 to the present to analyze carry returns in fixed and floating currency regimes. We first find that outsized carry returns occur exclusively in the floating regime, being zero in the fixed regime. Second, we show that fixed-to-floating regime shifts are associated with negative returns to a carry strategy implemented only on floating currencies, robust to the inclusion of volatility risks. These shifts are typically characterized by global flight-to-safety events that represent bad times for carry traders.

papers.title: Carry Trade, Forward Premium Puzzle and Currency Crisis
Crash-o-phobia in Currency Carry Trade Returns
Salvaging the C-CAPM: Currency Carry Trade Risk Premia and Conditioning Information
papers.authors: Abhay Abhyankar, Angelica Gonzalez, Olga Klinkowska
papers.abstract: We use a standard consumption-based asset pricing model incorporating conditioning information to explain the risk-return profile of currency carry trade portfolios. We use a scaled stochastic discount factor instead of scaled or managed portfolio returns as in previous work. Our conditioning variable is a forward-looking measure of net foreign assets. It arises from an intertemporal budget constraint and has predictive power for exchange rates. We find that our conditional consumption-CAPM is able to price a large part of the variation in cross-section of carry trade portfolios using cross-sectional as well as time series regression-based tests. Taken together, our results imply that the consumption-based models do still have a role to play in explaining excess returns on carry trade strategies.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Yield Curve Dynamics: A Fractal Framework for Improving Currency Carry Trade Return Distributions
Using Option-Implied Information to Improve Currency Carry Trade Profits
Asymetrix Currency Turbulence with Usdjpy Carry Trade: Insights into Central Bank Interventions and Exchange-Rate Dynamics
Currency Carry Trade Portfolios and Its Sensitivity to Interest Rates
The Impact of Currency Carry Trade Activity on the Transmission of Monetary Policy
papers.authors: Maximilian Boeck, Alina Steshkova, Thomas O. Zörner
papers.abstract: This paper examines how carry trade activity affects the transmission of monetary policy in currency markets. It analyzes a set of developed and emerging market currencies against the U.S. dollar. The U.S. dollar appreciates in response to a conventional monetary policy shock but depreciates to a central bank information shock. A threshold vector autoregressive model is fitted to discriminate between different regimes of speculative carry trade activity. Higher carry trade intensity is associated with larger excess returns and higher crash risk. Across regimes, the differences in exchange rates are mild, while those in interest rates are more pronounced. A currency trading strategy created on the day of central bank announcements, which takes into consideration the joint co-movement of interest rates and stock prices, substantially outperforms the carry trade in terms of the Sharpe ratio and downside risk.

papers.title: Currency Carry Trade by Trucks: The Curious Case of China's Massive Imports from Itself
papers.authors: Xuepeng Liu, Heiwai Tang, Zhi Wang, Shang-Jin Wei
papers.abstract: With capital controls, the standard financial market transactions needed for currency carry trade are hard to implement. Using detailed trade data reported by both the mainland Chinese and Hong Kong’s governments, we present evidence that indirect currency carry trade likely takes place via round-trip reimports. We also show that greater state control in terms of more state-owned firms does not reduce such “carry trade by trucks.”

papers.title: Half a Century of Risk Premia in a Generalized Multi-Currency Carry Strategy: An Empirical Investigation
papers.authors: Riccardo Rebonato, Riccardo Ronzani, Xuan Feng
papers.abstract: We study empirically the excess returns from a generalization of the traditional interest-rate and FX carry strategies in which the domestic, funding and investment currencies can all be different – a situation of great practical relevance. We express these excess returns in terms of economically interpretable covariances between forwards/futures ratio and the domestic stochastic discount factor. We find that these excess returns are predictable, and we make use of this predictability to create fullyout-of-sample state-dependent generalized strategies that display much higher Sharpe ratios, and much lower drawdowns, than the unconditional ones. We show that these conditional strategies benefit importantly from the ability to invest and fund in currencies different from the domestic one.

papers.title: Information-Geometric Phase Transitions in Currency Markets: Curvature-Driven Detection and Early Warning of Carry Trade Crashes in USD/JPY
papers.abstract: We propose a geometric framework to detect and forecast currency market dislocations, relying on the IG perspective of the macro-financial state variables. We employ the set of daily data from January 2010 to November 2025 to compute a curvature signal, Kt, which we obtain by rolling principal component embeddings of eight macro-financial variables relevant to the USD-JPY carry trade, namely, the spot log-return, the realized volatility, the U.S.-Japan short rate spread, the slope of the U.S. and Japan yield curves, the VIX, the deviations from covered interest parity, and a volatility-adjusted proxy of the carry regime. Kt takes negative values whenever the manifold of the market state variables exhibits concavity, which we have shown to be associated with tightening conditions, forward-spot misalignments, or constraints to global yen funding markets. We show that the negative curvature signal Kt consistently predicts the onset of all major USD-JPY carry unwind events, such as the COVID-19, the YCC stress/Fed tightening event of October 2022, the global funding shock of August 2024, as well as all historically identified yen flash events, without any false positives during periods of normal carry regimes. We also include the absolute CIP deviation, the absolute interest rate differential, and the VIX as additional regressors for the construction of the composite curvature-adjusted global risk index, GXCI-JP Y. The GXCI-JP Y has spiking activity exclusively at dislocation points, while the state space is divided into three geometrically distinct clusters corresponding to the safe, stressed, and crash regimes. We also prove the practical importance of the curvature by proposing the following simple yet transparent trading rule: long USD/JPY when Kt >-1.5 and GXCI-JP Y < 1.0, otherwise flat or short. The proposed trading rule results in an impressive 1,920% cumulative return between 2011 and November 2025, with a Sharpe ratio of 2.34 and a Calmar ratio of 19.8, outperforming the benchmark for carry, value, and momentum strategies. This proves that the information-geometric structure of the macro-financial state space has access to the leading-order information for the phase transition of the currency markets, thus providing a novel tool for the diagnosis of the risk, fragility, and carry trade of the global funding markets.

papers.title: Carry Trade and Precautionary Saving of Foreign Currency Debt: Evidence from Korean Firms
papers.authors: Steve Pak Yeung Wu, Annie Soyean Lee

papers.title: Currency Carry, Momentum, and Global Interest Rate Volatility
papers.abstract: Returns to currency carry and momentum compensate for the risk of global interest rate volatility (IRV), with risk exposures explaining 92% of the cross-sectional return variations. This unified explanation stems from its impact on FX intermediaries. An intermediary-based exchange rate model shows that a higher global IRV increases the uncertainty of future risk-taking and tightens current financial constraints. Position unwinding triggers loss of carry and momentum. Additional empirical results confirm this economic channel. Global IRV risk is also negatively priced in other currency strategies and momentum. The explanatory power is not driven by existing measures of uncertainty or intermediary constraints.

papers.title: When Carry Goes Bad: The Magnitude, Causes, and Duration of Currency Carry Unwinds
Technology Diffusion and Currency Carry Trades
Currency Regimes, Volatility Risks, and Carry Trades: The Option Value of Government Currency Intervention in Emerging Markets
Global foreign exchange volatility, ambiguity, and currency carry trades *

papers.title: Foreign Currency Borrowing of Corporations as Carry Trades: Evidence from India
papers.abstract: We establish that macroprudential policies limiting capital flows can curb risks arising from corporate foreign currency borrowing in emerging markets. Using detailed firm-level data from India, we show that propensity to issue foreign currency debt for the same firm is higher when the difference in short-term interest rates between India and the US is higher, i.e., when the dollar ‘carry trade’ is more profitable; this behavior is driven by the period after the global financial crisis. The positive relationship between issuance and the ‘carry trade’ breaks down once regulators institute more stringent interest-rate caps on foreign currency borrowing. Riskier borrowers such as importers and those with higher interest costs cut issuance most. Firm equity exposure to foreign exchange risk rose after issuance in favorable funding conditions and emerged as a source of external sector vulnerability during the ‘taper tantrum’ of 2013. Macroprudential policy action limiting capital flows is able to nullify this effect, such as during the market stress due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

papers.title: Currency Carry Trades and the Conditional Factor Model
The Shape of Carry: Construction, Leverage, and Crash Risk Across Currency and Bond Markets
papers.abstract: Carry strategies-holding higher-yielding assets financed by lower-yielding ones-earn a persistent premium that survives the assets' apparent riskiness. We build and backtest carry in two markets from primary data: a cross-sectional G10 currency factor and a four-sleeve U.S. fixed-income book spanning Treasuries, investment-grade and high-yield credit, and emerging-market sovereigns, monthly over 2001-2026. In both markets the unlevered premium is real but modest, with a Sharpe ratio near 0.5, and it is paid in an awkward currency: a thin profit in most months interrupted by rare, severe losses that cluster in funding crises. The currency factor's monthly skewness is-1.2; the high-yield sleeve's is-2.5. The practical problem, we argue, is not maximising carry but constructing it. Chasing yield delivers the highest return and the worst tail-levered four times, the naive bond book draws down more than 80%. Spreading exposure across carry sources whose crashes are imperfectly synchronised, and in fixed income holding the Treasury leg that rallies precisely when credit collapses, raises risk-adjusted return and drives equity beta toward zero. Volatility-targeting and drawdown control are not refinements; they are what makes the premium investable.

papers.title: Exploiting Overestimated Volatility Risk Premium: A Contrarian ETF Trading Strategy
papers.abstract:
This paper presents a contrarian trading strategy that leverages the Volatility Risk Premium (VRP) for trading ETFs such as SVXY, VIXY, SPY, and QQQ. The study hypothesizes that the VRP is often overestimated by the market, creating profitable trading opportunities. By buying or selling these ETFs based on specific VRP conditions, the strategy exploits mean reversion in market volatility to achieve superior risk-adjusted returns.

The paper outlines the theoretical foundation, empirical methodology, and performance evaluation through rigorous backtesting and real-time paper trading. Results show that leveraging an overestimated VRP significantly enhances portfolio performance, with the strategy yielding an average annual return of 20.79% and a Sharpe ratio of 1.4, outperforming traditional benchmarks.

This research contributes to volatility trading literature and provides practical insights for investors. Future research could explore the strategy’s applicability in different market environments and refine VRP predictions using machine learning techniques.

papers.title: Trading the Volatility Risk Premium on Nifty 50: Strategy Backtest with Realistic Frictions
papers.abstract: Systematic sellers of variance risk on U.S. equity index options have long earned a positive risk premium, but whether that premium survives realistic transaction costs in an emerging market with a high Securities Transaction Tax (STT) and wide bid-ask spreads remains an open question. This paper tests four short-volatility strategies on Nifty 50 index options over 119 monthly expiry cycles from January 2015 to April 2025, applying a cost model that incorporates STT (0.05% on sell-side premium), brokerage (0.03% per leg), slippage (0.5% of premium), and, for the deltahedged variant, daily futures rebalancing costs (0.01% per trade). The four strategies examined are an ATM short straddle, a crash-neutral spread, a naked put-write at four moneyness levels (k = 0.94, 0.96, 0.98, 1.00), and a delta-hedged straddle. Net of all costs, every strategy produces negative annualized returns. The put-write at k = 0.94 is the least adverse outcome, with a 91.6% monthly win rate and an annualized return of-0.9% (Sharpe ratio-0.37); the straddle variants lose approximately 44 to 45% per year. Cost attribution confirms that transaction costs are a secondary factor; the primary driver of losses across all strategies is tail risk, with single-month drawdowns reaching-13.2% of margin for the straddle variants and-18.3% for the k = 0.98 put-write (Table 1). These findings imply that the volatility risk premium documented in Pillai (2026a) exists in Indian index options but is not capturable by a retail trader under current market microstructure.

papers.title: Shorting Volatility: Harvesting the Risk Premium and Managing Tail Risk
papers.abstract: Short volatility strategies, which profit when market volatility remains subdued, have grown popular for their high average returns. They exploit the volatility risk premium (VRP), the persistent gap between implied and realized volatility[1]. Sellers of index options, for instance, historically earned steady profits as at-the-money S&P 500 straddles lost about 3% per week for buyers[2]. Using historical data and recent events, we show that short volatility positions deliver strong risk-adjusted returns—often rivaling or exceeding the equity risk premium—but are vulnerable to rare, extreme losses. One inverse volatility note returned over 1,000% from 2010–2017 (about 40% annually)[3], yet collapsed by more than 90% during the February 2018 “Volmageddon” spike[4]. The VRP has remained positive for decades[5][6], making short volatility an attractive income source. Still, its tail risk can exacerbate financial instability, as seen in 2018 and 2020, highlighting the importance of disciplined risk management for investors and regulators.

papers.title: Volatility Negative Impact: Risk Premium or Uncertainty
papers.abstract: We investigate the impact of volatility, as measured by the US VIX, on future investment growth. While the VIX can reflect both risk aversion and uncertainty, our findings suggest that the predominant effect on investment decisions arises from heightened risk aversion or an increased risk premium rather than from the uncertainty channel alone. Using regression analyses, we examine the differential responses of investment flows in the US to changes in the VIX and US industrial production.

papers.title: A Review of "The Volatility Risk Premium in the Oil Market"
papers.abstract: Hilary Till presented on this topic at the Commodity and Energy Markets Association conference in Budapest. She provided a brief description of the paper, "The Volatility Risk Premium in the Oil Market," followed by discussing the paper's (a) respect for data quality, (b) market microstructure insights, (c) end-investor insights, and (d) structural-break analysis.

papers.title: Global implied volatility and variance risk premium
papers.authors: Abdulkarim Alhejaili, Stefano Soccorsi, Katerina Tsakou
papers.abstract: Motivated by the global nature of financial risk, we propose a simple measure of global implied volatility (GIV) and show that it better describes international financial market dynamics than the VIX. Predictive evidence on both realized and implied volatilities around the world leads to the conclusion of truly global risk dynamics, not merely US spillovers. A direct global measure of variance risk premium based on GIV predicts expected excess returns in various international equity markets outperforming a previously proposed measure based on cross-market aggregation of local variance risk premia. We show that this is due to the international price of jump risk which is better captured by our global measure of variance risk premium. Foreign exchange markets confirm our findings. Currency portfolios based on our global variance risk premium generate significant value in excess of those based on aggregated local variance risk premia and the US variance risk premium.

papers.title: Discrete-Time Stochastic Volatility Models, the CBOE VIX1D and One-day Volatility Risk Premium
papers.authors: Wen Xu, Pakorn Aschakulporn, Jin E. Zhang
papers.abstract: The recent introduction of the one-day volatility index (VIX1D) by the Chicago Board Options Exchange reveals a persistently positive short-term volatility risk premium (VRP). This empirical finding underscores the importance of pricing short-term volatility risk and challenges Generalized Auto-Regressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) models, which imply a zero one-day VRP under the local risk-neutral valuation relationship (LRNVR). Motivated by this inconsistency, we propose a hybrid VIX1Dimplied stochastic volatility-in-mean (VSVM) model to demonstrate that the LRNVR assumption does not hold under a stochastic volatility framework, enabling the VSVM model to better capture the dynamics of the one-day VRP.

papers.title: Jump-Diffusion Long-Run Risks Models, Variance Risk Premium, and Volatility Dynamics
papers.abstract: This paper calibrates a class of jump-diffusion long-run risks (LRR) models to quantify how well they can jointly explain the equity risk premium and the variance risk premium in the U.S. financial markets, and whether they can generate realistic dynamics of risk-neutral and realized volatilities. I provide evidence that the jump risk in volatility of long run consumption growth is a key component of the equity risk premium and the variance risk premium in financial markets. Moreover, I find that matching the VIX dynamics during the calibration process is crucial when comparing different jump channels. Specifically, a jump-in-growth LRR model generates a good fit of the average variance risk premium, but a poor fit of the dynamics of the VIX or realized stock volatility. In contrast, a jump-in-volatility LRR model generates a smaller variance risk premium but better fits the VIX and the realized stock volatility dynamics. Finally, jump-in-volatility models generate predictability of returns by the variance risk premium that is more consistent with the data.

papers.title: Volatility Feedback and Risk Premium in GARCH Models with Generalized Hyperbolic Distributions
papers.abstract: The mixture structure of the generalized hyperbolic distribution of Barndorff-Nielsen (1997) is explored to quantify the contemporaneous correlation between return and volatility and to identify the effects of volatility feedback and risk premium within GARCH models. The statistical analysis of FTSE 100 and S&P 500 index excess return series supports both volatility feedback and risk premium theories.

papers.title: One-Day Volatility Indices and the Variance Risk Premium in European Equity Markets
papers.abstract: Daily-expiry index options have traded on Eurex since 2023, but Europe has no volatility benchmark for this horizon. Using one-minute Eurex order-book data, this paper constructs one-day model-free implied-variance indices-SX5E1D for the EURO STOXX 50 and DAX1D for the DAX-and estimates the associated variance risk premium. The premium is measured not from the index but from a calendar-time variance-swap rate matched exactly to futures-based realised variance, avoiding an overnight horizon mismatch. The mean implied-minus-realised volatility difference is 2.5 and 3.4 annualised percentage points. Valuing the strip at the seller's bid cuts the mean spread by 48% and 34%, leaving a positive average in both markets but only marginally so for the EURO STOXX 50. The indices track the 30-day benchmarks closely in levels but not in daily changes, which correlate at only 0.56. That variation is predictive, lifting the explanatory power of a next-day variance forecast by about twenty-five percentage points.

papers.title: Forecasting Equity Risk Premium: The Role of Investor Concern on Oil Price Volatility
Equity Risk Premium and Volatility: A European Perspective
Bond Yield Volatility Innovation and Equity Risk Premium
Rebuilding an Equity Volatility Surface from Public Data: Reliability and the Variance Risk Premium
papers.abstract: This paper rebuilds an equity volatility surface from free, public option data, asks how far it can be trusted, and trades the variance risk premium against it as a worked example. From raw quotes through cleaning, forward extraction, implied-volatility inversion and SVI calibration, the pipeline recovers a known surface exactly on synthetic inputs, so the errors that matter in practice are the data's, concentrated in the wings and the short end. The premium is visible without any model: over 2005 to 2026, VIX exceeded subsequent realised volatility on 85% of days. A short delta-hedged straddle harvests it, with the daily profit and loss attributed to the greeks. The strategy is profitable in a pre-registered development and hold-out split, but the figures are an upper bound, not an edge, resting on VIX as the implied level, a daily rehedge, and costs that omit the real frictions. The components are all established; the contribution is the reliability audit and the honest, pre-registered accounting.

papers.title: Early Birds Get the Vol: Morning Volatility Uncertainty and Variance Risk Premium
papers.abstract: We document that morning volatility-of-volatility (VVIX), measured at 10:00 EST during the U.S.-European market overlap, strongly predicts next-day variance asset returns. Predictive power peaks with t-statistics reaching 5.6 and adjusted R 2 of 2.6%, but diminishes after 11:00 EST. Trading strategies exploiting this pattern generate Sharpe ratios exceeding 2.0, remaining economically meaningful even after transaction costs. Crucially, intraday returns display a flat relationship with morning VVIX on high volatility uncertainty days, while close-to-close returns exhibit strong predictability. These findings are difficult to reconcile with standard risk premium theories but are consistent with limited attention and slow-moving beliefs about volatility.

papers.title: Asymmetric Covariance, Volatility, and Time-Varying Risk Premium: Evidence from the Finnish Stock Market
papers.abstract: It turns out that stock return volatility responds asymmetrically following negative stock returns. A negative return shock causes next-period volatility to increase more than that of a positive return shock. The article examines the asymmetric property of return volatility using the volatility feedback hypothesis in the context of the Finnish stock market index (OMXH25). Employing ADCC-EGARCH in modeling conditional covariance, results reveal that volatility feedback effect is weakly evident in the market although asymmetric effects increase covariance risk. However, the study finds evidence of significant idiosyncratic conditional volatility caused by either firm-level leverage and/or market inefficiency.

papers.title: The Variance Risk Premium: Model-Free Measurement, Term Structure, and the Economics of Selling Volatility
papers.abstract: Option-implied variance on the S&P 500 tends to run higher than the variance that ends up realized. In this paper, we derive the model-free measurement apparatus underlying that fact from first principles. The derivation starts with log-contract replication of realized variance via Itô's lemma. We then prove the Carr-Madan spanning identity. Finally, we build the exact discretization bridge to the CBOE's VIX formula. We then measure the resulting variance risk premium over 22 years of daily S&P 500 and VIX data (2004-2026). To do this, we use a forward-window realized-variance convention argued to be the only construction consistent with the premium's economic meaning. The premium averages approximately 3.5 volatility points. It is positive on 84% of sample days, and has a left-skewed distribution (skewness-7 in variance units). Additionally, its sign inverts during the global financial crisis, though not in every crisis regime in the sample. A VIX futures term structure built over 2007-2026 shows contango on 82% of days. It mirrors the same premium from a second instrument. A short-volatility strategy constructed from that curve illustrates the premium's economic payoff profile which is steady accumulated gains punctuated by catastrophic single-day losses. Section 6 relates these findings to a companion paper on rough volatility. It draws the line between what path roughness explains about this premium and what it leaves untouched.

papers.title: Learning and Forecasts about Option Returns through the Volatility Risk Premium
papers.authors: Alejandro Bernales, Louisa Chen, Marcela Valenzuela
papers.abstract: We use learning in an equilibrium model to explain the puzzling predictive power of the volatility risk premium (VRP) for option returns. In the model, a representative agent follows a rational Bayesian learning process in an economy under incomplete information with the objective of pricing options. We show that learning induces dynamic differences between probability measures P and Q, which produces predictability patterns from the VRP for option returns. The forecasting features of the VRP for option returns, obtained through our model, exhibit the same behaviour as those observed in an empirical analysis with S&P 500 index options.

papers.title: Liquidity Guided Machine Learning: The Case of the Volatility Risk Premium
papers.authors: Eric Ghysels, Ruslan Goyenko, Chengyu Zhang
papers.abstract: The financial industry has eagerly adopted machine learning algorithms to improve on traditional predictive models. In this paper we caution against blindly applying such techniques. We compare forecasting ability of machine learning methods in evaluating future payoffs on synthetic variance swaps. Standard machine learning methods tend to identify contracts which are illiquid, and hard to trade. The most successful strategies turn out to be those where we pair machine learning with institutional and market/traders inputs and insights. We show that liquidity guided pre-selection of inputs to machine learning results in trading strategies with improved pay-offs to the writers of variance swap contract replicating portfolio.

papers.title: Belief Uncertainty, Volatility Risk Premium, and Speculative Trading
Multiscale Stochastic Volatility Problem With Wavelet Risk Premium
papers.authors: Bright Okore Osu, Chidinma Olunkwa, M.E. Egwe, Festus N. Chuku
papers.abstract: In this paper, the mean variance portfolio with multiscale stochastic volatility using the wavelet risk premium was considered. A seemingly wavelet function which was used to investigate the multiscale stochastic volatility(MSSV) used in stock price model was derived. Two types of volatility, namely; a fast -moving one and a slowly-moving one were considered using the stochastic dynamic programming principle and\\ Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation approach. The optimal investment strategy, the value function was obtained.

papers.title: GARCH-M Model With an Asymmetric Risk Premium: Distinguishing Between ‘Good’ and ‘Bad’ Volatility Periods
Very Noisy Option Prices and Inference Regarding the Volatility Risk Premium
papers.authors: Jefferson Duarte, Christopher S. Jones, Junbo L. Wang
papers.abstract:
The stylized fact that volatility is not priced in individual equity options does not
withstand scrutiny. We show, first, that the average return of heavily traded deep
out-of-the-money call options on stocks is -116 basis points per day. Second, Fama-
MacBeth estimates of the volatility risk premium in stock options are similar to
those in S&P 500 Index call options. Third, the mean return of heavily traded
delta-hedged ATM calls (puts) is -23 (-30) basis points. Fourth, the variance risk
premium in stock options is negative. Our analysis highlights the importance of
microstructure biases and robustness in empirical work with options.

papers.title: Harvesting the Downside Beta Premium with the Implied Volatility Term Structure: The Cinderella Strategy
