Which Mechanism, Illiquidity or Volatility Risk, Better Explains the Equity Premium Puzzle?
Instantaneous Volatility and the Liquidity Premium
papers.abstract: I investigate how transaction costs affect the optimal portfolio policy when volatility is stochastic. I find an analytical expression of the minimal size of the no trade region. This enables us to analyze the liquidity premium related to instantaneous volatility. I find the liquidity premium to be time dependent. With a finite investment horizon, the liquidity premium increases as the investment horizon approaches. I also find that the size of the liquidity premium is twice as large if the correlation between the stock returns and the volatility is zero. Contrary to findings in standard literature, I find that the risk aversion plays a significant role in determining the size of the liquidity premium. To the best of our knowledge, I am the first to analyze the impact of stochastic volatility on the liquidity premium. The results indicate that the transaction costs have a first-order effect on the liquidity premium.

papers.title: Information Environment and Equity Risk Premium Volatility Around the World
papers.authors: Sie Ting Ting Lau, Lilian K. Ng, Bohui Zhang

papers.title: A Tactical Strategy using ETFs: Harvesting Volatility Risk Premia & Crisis Alpha
papers.abstract: I discuss a systematic approach to investing in volatility risk premia through ETFs. The reason behind ETFs is mostly due to my personal interest in volatility investing and being able to manage the risk of the strategy on my own without any capital constraint. However, I will be using futures contracts mostly to backfill the data for my backtest but the main idea is focused around futures contracts whose exposure can be obtained through ETFs. I construct a primary model for harvesting volatility risk premia and next overlay a meta model for risk management using ridge regression. I also incorporate a CTA program using selected commodity ETFs to harvest crisis alpha.

papers.title: Liquidity Premium, Liquidity-Adjusted Return and Volatility, and Extreme Liquidity
papers.abstract: We establish innovative liquidity premium measures, and construct liquidity-adjusted return and volatility to model assets with extreme liquidity, represented by a portfolio of selected crypto assets, and upon which we develop a set of liquidity-adjusted ARMA-GARCH/EGARCH models. We demonstrate that these models produce superior predictability at extreme liquidity to their traditional counterparts. We provide empirical support by comparing the performances of a series of Mean Variance portfolios.

papers.title: WINTER BLUES OR MONETARY NEWS? INTEREST RATE SEASONALITY AND STOCK RETURNS
papers.abstract: We revisit factors associated with seasonality of stock markets. We find that interest rates and their seasonal components exhibit a strong relationship with returns and that association is more pronounced in countries, where interest rate seasonality is generally small. Additionally, using difference-in-difference estimation, we add to the growing evidence of increased synchronicity among countries belonging to the European Monetary Union. While we find strong evidence for stock market relationship with economic factors, our sample exhibits little indication that changing risk preferences throughout the year affect seasonality in stock returns.

papers.title: Decomposing Option Anomaly Returns
Seasonality, Academic Calendar and School Drop-Outs in South Asia
Seasonality in Stock Returns: Evidence from Advanced Emerging Stock Markets
papers.authors: Mostafa Seif, Paul Docherty, Abul Shamsuddin
papers.abstract: Despite an extensive number of studies documenting evidence of seasonal anomalies in developed markets, only a few studies have comprehensively examined these anomalies within emerging markets. Testing the robustness of seasonal anomalies in emerging markets would first, help to examine the theoretical explanations that have been proposed and second, provide an out-of-sample result for these seasonality anomalies. This study examines the efficiency of advanced emerging markets by testing five seasonal anomalies: the month of the year, other January, day-of-the-week, holiday, and week 44. Evidence is reported that is consistent with all of these seasonal anomalies with the exception of the other January effect; supporting the argument that advanced emerging markets are less than perfectly efficient.

papers.title: A Trading-Status Filter Drops Delisting Returns from CRSP’s CIZ Daily File: Consequences for Anomaly Returns
papers.abstract: CRSP’s CIZ daily file stores a delisted stock’s final return on a separate record marked as not trading, so a filter that keeps only active trading days removes it. For CRSP common stocks, 1926–2025, adding back the recorded delisting returns lowers equal-weighted size and reversal spreads by 5 to 6 basis points a month and raises the momentum spread by 9. With missing involuntary returns set to -30%, the changes are 8 to 12 basis points; value-weighted spreads move by 3 or less.

papers.title: Anomaly Returns and FOMC
papers.authors: Lin Tan, Xiaoyan Zhang, Guofu Zhou
papers.abstract: We investigate anomaly return changes around Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) announcements. Across 179 anomalies, we document a negative drift of 5.71 bps in long-short returns on FOMC days, which begins to accrue in pre-announcement trading hours. This reversal is asymmetrically driven by a nearly 38-bp rally in short-leg returns. The drift can be explained by compensation for market risk, especially when incorporating jump risk. The decline is amplified by larger monetary policy surprises and related to interest rate shock exposures. Furthermore, institutions become net buyers of short-leg stocks on FOMC days, consistent with de-risking driven by limits to arbitrage.

papers.title: The Leverage Anomaly in U.S. Bank Stock Returns
papers.abstract: The relationship between leverage and returns on US bank stocks between 1973 and 2019 is slightly hump-shaped, almost flat. This observed relationship cannot be explained by standard risk factors such as correlation with the market return, book-to-market, size, momentum and term structure of interest rates. As a result, risk-adjusted returns (alphas) of highly leveraged banks are negative. Moreover, the stock returns exhibit a delayed reaction to changes in leverage. Highly leveraged banks that further increase their debt have high abnormal returns on the day of announcement, but tend to have low risk-adjusted returns during the following 6 months. This paper uncovers several explanations for this leverage anomaly. First, investors seem to underestimate the negative effect of leverage on future asset growth. Next, under-priced default risk, under-priced systematic risk and sensitivity to idiosyncratic volatility are prominent features of bank stock returns.

papers.title: The Zodiac Calendar and Equity Factor Returns
papers.abstract: We calculate the returns for four well-known equity factor returns, the market, size, value, and momentum, for each Zodiac calendar year from 1926 to 2015. We find that point estimates of average returns for each Zodiac sign can be substantially different. However, when we employ statistical tests, we do not find enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis of equal excess returns across Zodiac signs. For an investor with an equally-weighted portfolio in these four equity factors, the Year of the Rooster may seem particularly good and the Year of the Ox particularly poor, but also in this case the null hypothesis cannot be rejected. Hence, we conclude that investment strategies based on Zodiac signs are unlikely to generate superior returns.

papers.title: Seasonality in Government Bond Returns and Factor Premia
Quartile-Based Seasonality Decomposition for Time Series Forecasting and Anomaly Detection
The Election Anomaly in Bitcoin Returns
papers.authors: Savva Shanaev, Bogdan Maksikov, Mikhail Vasenin
papers.abstract: This study discovers a statistically and economically significant anomaly in Bitcoin performance-returns are, on average, 2.2% higher on major election days in G20 democracies on an exhaustive 2010-2024 sample that includes a full Bitcoin price history and 60 election events. This price appreciation is shown to be permanent, independent of the election outcome, and it is not accompanied by any significant prior or subsequent abnormal returns. The effect cannot be explained by conventional calendar anomalies or the Bitcoin halving cycle, and it is robust to alternative specifications and weighting schemes. The documented anomaly highlights the importance of cryptocurrencies in hedging political risks and presents a profitable trading opportunity for investors.

papers.title: In Search of Seasonality in Intraday and Overnight Option Returns
papers.authors: Turan G. Bali, Amit Goyal, Mathis Moerke, Florian Weigert

papers.title: Earnings Seasonality, Management Earnings Forecasts, and Stock Returns
papers.authors: Danling Jiang, Pan Song, Hongquan Zhu

papers.title: Daily Seasonality of US Capital Market’s Returns in the Time Intervals Associated to the Halloween Effect
Daily Seasonality of London Stock Exchange Returns in the Time Intervals Associated to the Halloween Effect
Being Surprised by the Unsurprising: Earnings Seasonality and Stock Returns
papers.authors: Tom Chang, Samuel M. Hartzmark, David H. Solomon, Eugene F. Soltes
papers.abstract: We present evidence consistent with markets failing to properly price information in seasonal earnings patterns. Firms with historically larger earnings in one quarter of the year (“positive seasonality quarters”) have higher returns when those earnings are usually announced. Analysts have more positive forecast errors in positive seasonality quarters, consistent with the returns being driven by mistaken earnings estimates. We show that investors appear to overweight recent lower earnings following positive seasonality quarters, leading to pessimistic forecasts in the subsequent positive seasonality quarter. The returns are not explained by risk-based explanations, firm-specific information, increased volume, or idiosyncratic volatility.

papers.title: From the Stars to the Stock Market: Calendar Superstition and IPO Returns
papers.abstract: The ancient Chinese Almanac lists days that are (in)auspicious for certain actions or events. We find that the initial returns for Initial Public Offerings (IPO), an essential corporate event, are significantly lower on days listed by the Almanac as unlucky. The effect of calendar superstition is robust after controlling for a preference for lucky numbers (such as lucky listing codes and prices) and is more pronounced among firms with high investment risks and firms located in places where superstition culture is more prominent. Our results suggest that investor risk perception, but not manager superstition, plays a vital role in determining the calendar superstition effect.

papers.title: Learning from Anomaly Distributions: Expected Returns and Limits to Arbitrage
papers.abstract: Anomalies that predict stock returns are typically treated independently, even though investors observe many correlated signals simultaneously. We develop a top-down framework for statistical limits to arbitrage that examines how the cross-anomaly distribution, rather than individual signals, shapes expected returns. In the model, anomaly signals are noisy observations of a latent mispricing component, and arbitrageurs solve a signal-extraction problem in which both mispricing and signal precision are jointly inferred. The framework predicts that when signal precision is heterogeneous, the informational content of higher-order moments depends on mean signal strength. Under strong signals, dispersion, skewness, and kurtosis increase posterior responsiveness to the mean signal, amplifying its effect on expected returns; under weak signals, they primarily capture noise. Using 140 anomaly measures for U.S. stocks over the 1971–2022 period, we construct cross-anomaly distributions and examine their moments. Dispersion, skewness, and kurtosis contain economically meaningful information beyond individual anomaly signals, including flexible nonlinear benchmarks. The predictive power arises mainly through interactions with the mean and among higher-order moments, consistent with a convex relation in posterior precision. Results are robust across market conditions, time periods, and alternative anomaly subsets. Portfolio tests using machine-learning and AP-Trees methods show that adding higher-order moments to the full set of individual anomalies increases out-of-sample abnormal returns net of transaction costs. Overall, the cross-anomaly distribution offers a parsimonious, interpretable representation of high-dimensional signals, with dispersion, asymmetry, and tail behavior containing predictive information beyond individual anomalies and standard risk factors, highlighting a novel source of statistical limits to arbitrage.

papers.title: Fading the Almanac: A Behavioral Reassessment of Calendar Seasonality in Spot Currency Markets The Deflated Alpha Series
papers.abstract:
Calendar seasonality — the claim that a given asset's returns are systematically higher or lower in
particular months, weeks, or days — is one of the oldest and most contested empirical regularities in
finance. This paper conducts two seasonality investigations in spot FX (EURUSD, GBPUSD, AUDUSD,
USDJPY), a market far less studied for calendar effects than equities, and reports both a
methodological cautionary tale and a substantive finding. We first document, as an opening case study,
a naive day-of-week/turn-of-month seasonality screen that not only fails on its own terms but
demonstrates — when retrofitted onto a near-miss intraday strategy from elsewhere in this series — a
concrete grid-design snooping mechanism: adding a five-level weekday filter as a free walk-forward
dimension causes a fold-level optimizer to chase noise and "discover" Monday as informative when, in
the full honest sample, Monday is in fact the worst-performing weekday. We then present a properly
designed successor study that trains an exact binomial sign test — the correct tool given only 2 to 8
yearly observations per calendar month, where a t-test's asymptotic assumptions do not remotely hold
— on rolling 2-, 5-, and 8-year trailing windows across the full symbol-month universe. Of 96 (symbol,
month, lookback) combinations tested, only four clear a defensible significance bar: EURUSD
February bearish, EURUSD and GBPUSD December bullish (a pattern independently corroborated by
well-documented year-end USD liquidity effects), and USDJPY June bullish. Pooling trades across all
four symbols, the resulting thin-sample backtest (13-18 trades per specification) shows that fading the
detected seasonal bias outperforms following it (expectancy +0.36R to +0.46R fading vs. -0.28R to
-0.40R following; permutation p ≈ 0.07-0.08) — the fourth independent instance, after the fibonacci-
pullback and liquidity-sweep/change-of-character findings reported in Papers 2 and 3 of this series, of
this research program's recurring meta-pattern that naive, textbook-obvious technical and calendar
narratives run backwards in this data. We connect this to the post-publication anomaly-decay
literature (McLean and Pontiff, 2016) and to overcrowded-positioning explanations for why a well-
advertised seasonal narrative might be more profitably faded than ridden. A supplementary exercise
applying the four identified biases since 2020 finds that a validated intraday timing signal (the
fibonacci-pullback-fade mechanism of Paper 2) restricted to fire only in the seasonally favored
direction outperforms naive buy-and-hold-the-season on two of three testable symbols, suggesting
seasonality is best treated as a directional filter layered onto a validated timing mechanism rather than
as a standalone strategy. We are explicit throughout that the sign-test detection finding and the
tradeability finding carry different confidence levels: the former is a correctly conducted, if modest,
statistical detection; the latter remains a suggestive, underpowered addendum.

papers.title: Can the Anomaly Zoo Speak with One Voice? Consensus, Reliability, and Expected Returns
papers.abstract: Using 212 signed Chen-Zimmermann/Open Asset Pricing predictors, this paper studies whether the anomaly zoo contains a common real-time expected-return signal and whether that signal has measurable reliability states. The empirical design starts in 1963, uses expanding training windows with fixed twelve-year validation windows, and predicts returns from 1985 through 2024. The robust consensus, denoted C * , aggregates a family of legitimate consensus makers rather than selecting a single winning model. C * predicts next-month stock returns in Fama-MacBeth regressions and value-weighted portfolio sorts. A value-weighted high-minuslow portfolio earns an FF5-plus-momentum alpha of 1.06 percent per month. The premium is systematically conditioned by model agreement, signal-profile shape, support quality, higher moments, attention, information resolution, limits-to-arbitrage states, and the location of information across industries and peers. The evidence shows that high-dimensional anomaly information is organized by both consensus and reliability. The anomaly zoo contains a common expected-return component, and the reliability state behind that component changes how the signal should be interpreted in asset-pricing tests and portfolio choice.

papers.title: Macroeconomic Fundamentals, Expected Returns and the Pricing of Anomaly Portfolios
papers.authors: Abhay Abhyankar, Rajesh Tharyan, Xiang Zhang
papers.abstract: Recent research has identified more than three hundred factors that have statistically significant prices of risk in asset pricing tests. This evidence is disconcerting and more parsimonious factor pricing models are required. Our work contributes to the effort of reducing this “zoo of factors”. We propose a set of empirical factors that mimic macroeconomic sources of risk in the economy. Our three factor model does well in explaining the cross-section of a number of common benchmark portfolios and other ‘anomaly’ spreads relative to standard empirical factor models.

papers.title: Calendar Anomaly and the Degree of Market Inefficiency of Bitcoin
The Accrual Anomaly in Australia: A Closer Look at Trading Strategy Returns
papers.abstract: We conduct a detailed examination of the accrual anomaly in Australia using a trading strategy research design. Our primary contribution is to show how sensitive the results are to the precise research design specifications. We focus on four key areas of importance in designing such tests. First, the choice of proxy for total accruals; second, the definition of abnormal returns (i.e., the return generating model); third, the impact of data trimming as a response to exceptionally large returns; and fourth, the choice between value or equal weighting of returns. We show that research design choices do matter, and in doing so we also provide some reconciliation of apparently conflicting prior evidence of any accrual anomaly in Australia. Our results suggest the need for caution in drawing inferences from specific research design specifications in trading strategy tests of the accrual anomaly.

papers.title: Changes in Ownership Breadth and Anomaly Returns
Calendar Effects on Stock Returns Across Multiple States
A Careful Re-Examination of Seasonality in International Stock Markets: Comment on Sentiment and Stock Returns
papers.authors: Mark J. Kamstra, Lisa A. Kramer, Maurice David Levi
papers.abstract: In questioning Kamstra, Kramer, and Levi’s (2003) finding of an economically and statistically significant seasonal affective disorder (SAD) effect, Kelly and Meschke (2010) make errors of commission and omission. They misrepresent their empirical results, claiming that the SAD effect arises due to a "mechanically induced" effect that is non-existent, labeling the SAD effect a "turn-of-year" effect (when in fact their models and ours separately control for turn-of-year effects), and ignoring coefficient-estimate patterns that strongly support the SAD effect. Our analysis of their data shows, even using their low-power statistical tests, there is significant international evidence supporting the SAD effect. Employing modern, panel/time-series statistical methods strengthens the case dramatically. Additionally, Kelly and Meschke represent the finance, psychology, and medical literatures in misleading ways, describing some findings as opposite to those reported by the researchers themselves, and choosing selective quotes that could easily lead readers to a distorted understanding of these findings.

papers.title: Intra-day Seasonality and Abnormal Returns in the Brent Crude Oil Futures Market
papers.authors: Christian Oliver Ewald, Erik Haugom, Ruolan Ouyang, Erik Smith-Meyer, Ståle Størdal

papers.title: Trading Volume, Anomaly Returns and Noise Trader Risk in China
Post-Earnings Announcement Drift and Drift-Period Systematic News
papers.abstract: Recent studies find that post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) is related to the business cycle. In this study, I examine how PEAD varies with drift-period systematic news. I find that PEAD is stronger when a firm’s earnings surprise is followed by drift-period systematic news of the same sign; PEAD is weaker, insignificant or reversed when a firm’s earnings surprise is followed by drift-period systematic news of the opposite sign. The relation between drift-period systematic news and PEAD cannot be explained by investor underreaction to past firm earnings news, the commonly accepted explanation for PEAD, or drift-period firm earnings news. Finally, the influence of systematic news on PEAD appears to arise from changes in real economic activity, rather than changes in investor sentiment.

papers.title: Post Earnings Announcement Drift, a Price Signal?
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the robustness of post-earnings-announcement-drift (PEAD) on a price signal perspective, unlike the traditional literature that focuses on fundamental signal. The studied period is 2003-2015, for four main US indices. The results suggest that some economic agents are too slow to integrate the information, although they still have a major market impact. We find a strong empirical evidence of the preeminence of this bias for Momentum stocks rather than blue-chips or non-Momentum small-caps. Even by challenging the strategy, the conclusion remains strong with abnormal returns linked to such market inefficiency, with better returns for positive signals than negative ones. We choose Nasdaq Composite as the backbone of our development as it is the closest index to Uncia’s field of expertise. For indices known as Momentum, we find strong predictability of the systematic net exposure, the latter being a consequence of the long and short positions implied by the earnings signals.

papers.title: Earnings Persistence Cliff and Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift
papers.abstract: We document a sharp persistence cliff in firm-level earnings surprises at the fiscal-year boundary. Earnings-surprise persistence is stable across quarter-to-quarter transitions within a fiscal year but declines markedly from FQ4 to the subsequent FQ1. We develop a regime-switching framework in which investors infer the persistence of earnings news from past surprises. Because the weak relation between FQ4 and FQ1 surprises leads investors to underestimate the persistence of FQ1 news, prices underreact to its implications for future earnings, generating stronger postearnings-announcement drift (PEAD). Consistent with this prediction, we find that the PEAD following FQ1 announcements is approximately 83% larger than following announcements in other fiscal quarters. The effect is robust across return horizons and sectors. Moreover, the FQ1 PEAD remains economically and statistically significant after the mid-2000s, even as the overall PEAD largely disappears. We also document similar persistence cliffs in other firm characteristics associated with investor underreaction. Our findings are not attributable to microcap firms, prior earnings-surprise streaks, calendar-year seasonality, or earnings management, nor are they subsumed by existing explanations for PEAD.

papers.title: Informed Trading Competition and The Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift
Investors' Limited Attention and Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
Visualizing Earnings to Predict Post-Earnings Announcement Drift: A Deep Learning Approach
Investors' Limited Attention and Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
Menu Effects and Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift in Chinese Stock Market
Credit Rating, Post-Earnings-Announcement-Drift, and Arbitrage from Transient Institutions
papers.abstract: This study first establishes a robust link between credit rating and post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD). I find strong evidence that PEAD is more salient for firms with low credit ratings. This finding is consistent with the notion that investors are prone to underreact to earnings news from low-credit-rating firms that are characterized by high uncertainty of asset fundamentals. The association between credit rating and PEAD is not driven by traditional information uncertainty proxies such as earnings volatility, cash flow volatility, accruals quality, firm age, idiosyncratic volatility, and analyst forecast dispersion. I further investigate whether transient institutions exploit the differential of PEAD among different rated firms in their arbitrage trades. The results reveal that transient institutions tend to focus their arbitrage on low-credit-rating firms. However, the existence and concentration of PEAD in low-credit-rating firms suggest that transient institutions fail to arbitrage away PEAD among low-rated firms and that the arbitrage strategy is riskier than expected by the transient institutions. This in turn implies that estimation risk associated with pricing the earnings news of low-rated firms plays a substantive role in forming the strong PEAD of these firms.

papers.title: The Post-Earnings-Announcement-Drift and Order Flows of Correlated Stocks
papers.abstract: The Post-Earnings-Announcements-Drift (PEAD) is one of the most persistent asset pricing anomalies and poses a challenge to the efficient market hypothesis. It states that the immediate stock price reaction to public earnings announcements does not fully reflect the true value of the stock, leaving the rest of the value to be discovered by investors’ trading. Past studies find that the earnings announcement has significant and positive spillover effect on the returns of stocks in the same industry which implies that investors with better understanding of stock values may choose to invest in these stocks if there is trading less friction. Similar to Easley, O’Hara and Srinivas (1998) who investigate the informational role of option volume to stock price, this paper investigates the informational role of order flows of non-announcing stocks in the same industry during the announcement window. I document three empirical findings. 1) The non-announcing stocks have similar drifts as the announcing stocks after an earnings announcement, majorly after positive earnings surprise announcement. 2) The order flows of non-announcing stocks in the same industry relative to that of announcing stocks have significant explanatory power for the PEAD of the announcing stocks. This relation is robust and significant after I control for a rich set of standard explanatory variables. 3) Illiquidity, as a measure of trading friction, explains a significant part of investors’ trading preference during the announcement window. Moreover, consistent with my hypothesis, the relation between net order flows is most pronounced in the subsample where event stock liquidity is the lowest compared to its industry peers.

papers.title: Exploiting Earnings Persistence to Better Measure Market Expectations in Detecting Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
papers.abstract: We construct an alternate proxy for earnings expectations that does not depend on analyst following and exploits differential earnings persistence across earnings levels. We examine the usefulness of our proxy in the context of post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) where the random walk model is still widely used in the literature. We show that a refined trading strategy using our alternative proxy results in statistically significant and economically large increases in PEAD relative to the random walk model. Furthermore, using a subsample where analysts’ forecasts are available, we show that the PEAD associated with our alternate proxy is incremental to the PEAD associated with analyst forecast errors. Our earnings expectation proxy can be used in other settings where extreme earnings or earnings surprise portfolios are the focus of the analysis and researchers want to include firms without analyst following.

papers.title: Firm Characteristics and the Cross-Sectional Variation in Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
papers.abstract: This paper explores which characteristics of a given firm have predictive power over the magnitude and persistence of post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) using both a machine learning framework and linear regression approach. Using Compustat quarterly fundamentals and CRSP daily returns for a sample of 6,728 U.S. firms over 2004 to 2023, we construct a panel of 203,764 firm-quarter earnings events and compute cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) over 21 and 63 trading-day post-announcement windows. Standardized unexpected earnings (SUE) are measured via a seasonal random walk model. We then train a LightGBM gradient boosted model alongside an OLS ridge regression in a walk-forward validation framework, predicting 1 month post-announcement drift from 13 firm characteristics. The gradient boosted model achieves an out of sample R^2 of 1.04%, generating a predicted Q5-Q1 portfolio spread of 4.29% over 21 trading days, exceeding the raw SUE-sorted spread of 3.27%; in calendar-time long-short portfolios this spread is statistically significant (Newey-West t-statistic of 19.3 across 60 quarterly cohorts). Short term pre-announcement momentum, book-to-market ratio (BTM ratio), and intermediate momentum are the strongest predictors of drift magnitude, while SUE itself ranks ninth, suggesting that how a firm arrives at an earnings surprise matters more than how large the surprise is. The LGBM model (interchangeably referred to as the gradient boosted or machine learning model) substantially outperforms the linear baseline (interchangeably referred to as the OLS model or ridge regression model, R^2 of-0.0003), indicating that the predictive relationships are fundamentally nonlinear.

papers.title: The Post Earnings Announcement Drift and Option Traders
papers.authors: Suresh Govindaraj, Sangsang Liu, Joshua Livnat
papers.abstract: The Post-Earnings Announcement Drift (PEAD) anomaly refers to the tendency of stock prices to continue drifting in the same direction as earnings surprises well through the subsequent earnings announcements; ignoring the autocorrelations in extreme earnings surprises across adjacent quarters. Currently, the two major competing theories to explain PEAD are: the risk premium hypothesis (RPH), which argues that the anomaly exists only because risk has been measured improperly; and, the under-reaction (behavioral) hypothesis (URH), which assumes investors do not completely utilize the auto-correlations of earnings surprises. We test the former (RPH) by using a finer metric for risk than used in prior research, namely, the change in implied volatilities obtained from options prices immediately before and after the earnings announcements. Inconsistent with the predictions of RPH: (1) we do not find a positive correlation between the implied volatility changes and earnings surprises; and (2) we find that implied volatilities (risk) actually decrease most after the earnings announcements for firms with the most positive earnings surprises. Using volatility based option trading strategies (straddles), we examine if option traders have a similar URH bias to those of equity traders. We find that option straddles based on extreme earnings surprises in the prior quarter are not more profitable than straddles on mild earnings surprises, indicating that option traders already incorporate the prior earnings surprise in option prices.

papers.title: Trading Frictions and the Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift
papers.authors: Josef Fink, Stefan Palan, Erik Theissen
papers.abstract: We use laboratory experiments to analyze how the existence of trading frictions (a transaction fee and a ban on short selling and margin buying) affects occurrence and strength of the post-earnings-announcement drift. We find lower trading activity and higher asset prices in the presence of frictions. While the initial price reaction to earnings announcements is weaker, the strength of the PEAD is not materially affected. Trading strategies aimed at exploiting the PEAD are less profitable in the presence of frictions.

papers.title: Prior-Biased Inference in Asset Prices: The Conditional Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
papers.abstract: I show that the post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD) is concentrated where the earnings surprise goes against analysts' recommendations. A recommendation-inconsistent strategy, long Sell-rated firms with positive surprises and short Buy-rated firms with negative surprises, earns a 9.4% abnormal return per annum. The recommendation-consistent counterpart is indistinguishable from zero. The PEAD has not disappeared: it survives in recommendation-inconsistent states, especially after bad news to optimistically-rated firms. A model combining overconfidence--which generates biased priors and leaves the largest mispricing when news contradicts them--with an asymmetrically muted response to bad news under optimistic priors rationalizes these patterns.

papers.title: Corporate Governance, Investor Attention and Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
papers.authors: xiaohan li, Guojun Wu, Canlin Li
papers.abstract: We study how corporate governance would affect market reactions to earnings surprises: the post-earnings announcement drift phenomenon. We conjecture that both investors’ under-reactions and over-reactions to earnings surprises can cause the post earnings announcement drift. For a bad governance firm, we conjecture that investors would under-react to earnings surprises as they are less confident in the earnings announcements and attribute the earnings surprises more to the firm's luck rather than to its ability, and it’s this under-reaction that causes the post announcement drift in a bad governance firm. In contrast, for a good governance firm we conjecture that as investors are more confident in its earnings surprises and attribute them more to the firm's ability rather than to its luck, their reactions to earnings surprises could change from under-reaction to over-reaction, and it’s this over-reaction that causes the drift in a good governance firm. Using earnings and firm characteristics data from I/B/E/S and Compustat together with corporate governance data we provide results supporting these conjectures.

papers.title: Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift in Brazilian Equities: Evidence from a Preregistered Event Study
papers.abstract: Earlier studies on Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift (PEAD) in Brazil did not use a preregistered method, and neither of the two main ones defined its sample by point-in-time index membership. This research tests Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift in Brazilian equities while having a design fixed and time-stamped before the results were computed. The universe is the point-in-time constituents of the Ibovespa and Small Caps indices from 2021-2025. Quarterly standardized unexpected earnings (SUE) are built from public CVM files, abnormal returns come from a market model, and three hypotheses were tested as one confirmatory family with Holm correction. The coverage includes 2,997 prices of 3,130 eligible quarter events (4.25% was missing, below the 5% preregistered ceiling), and 2,700 events are ranked into within-quarter SUE deciles across 20 calendar quarters. After the analysis, none of the three hypotheses is supported after the Holm adjustment. The trend of mean CAR [t+1, t+60] across SUE deciles is negative (nominal p = 0.185, Holm p = 0.369), and the top-minus-bottom decile spread is-2.07 percentage points (nominal p = 0.245, Holm p = 0.369). The spread is 5.09 percentage points higher in the lower-liquidity half of the sample, as H3 predicts (nominal p = 0.027), but this does not survive the family-wise correction (Holm p = 0.081). In other words, the biggest difference between good-news and bad-news stocks occurs by the announcement day (t = 0), and the negative 60-day spread is a result of a late recovery of the bad-news decile. The results show that a positive PEAD is not confirmed in Brazil under a preregistered design using five years of data.

papers.title: Investment Horizon of Shareholders and Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift
papers.authors: Min Kyeong Kwon, Tong Suk Kim
papers.abstract: We hypothesize that post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD) is caused by underreaction of long-term investors since they do not pay much attention to short-term events. Consistent with the hypothesis, empirical observations show that stocks mostly held by long-term investors exhibit strong PEAD, while stocks mostly held by short-term investors does not. The results are still robust even after transaction costs, investor recognition, temporal inattention, and reversal in earnings surprises are controlled for.

papers.title: Menu Effects and Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift in Chinese Stock Market
Drift or Jump: What Drives Post-Earnings Announcement Stock Returns?
papers.abstract: One of the contentious issues regarding the post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) is whether the abnormal stock return is driven by investors’ delayed reaction to earnings information or by unexpected information shocks subsequent to earnings announcement. In this paper, we disentangle unexpected large changes in stock prices, known as jumps, from total stock returns. Although on average jump occurs only once per firm quarter, it accounts for up to 40% of the return differential between top and bottom SUE deciles. This is evidence that a significant part of PAED is driven by unexpected information shocks. Nevertheless, the drift component still explains at least 50% of the variation of anomalous PEAD returns. The findings suggest that PEAD cannot be entirely attributed to investors’ delayed reaction to earnings information, but neither can the hypothesis be ruled out. In particular, we find that delayed reaction is more pronounced following positive earnings surprises.

papers.title: Post Earnings Announcement Drift and Price Impact Around Earnings Announcements Evidence from London Stock Exchange1
papers.authors: Sijia Zhang, Qiuling Hua, He Wu

papers.title: Asymmetric Learning from Prices and Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
papers.authors: Jaewon Choi, Linh Thompson, Jared Williams
papers.abstract: Motivated by research in psychology and experimental economics, we assume that investors update their beliefs about an asset's value upon observing the price, but only when the price clearly reveals that others obtained private information that differs from their own private information. In particular, we assume that investors learn from the price of an asset in an asymmetric manner--they learn from the price if they observe good (bad) private information and the price is worse (better) than what is justified based on public information alone. We show that asymmetric learning from an asset's price leads to post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD), and that it generates arbitrage opportunities that are less attractive than alternative explanations of PEAD. In addition, our model predicts that PEAD will be concentrated in earnings surprises that are not dominated by accruals, and it also predicts that earnings response coefficients will decline in the magnitude of the earnings surprises.

papers.title: Herding on Earnings News: The Role of Institutional Investors in Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift
papers.authors: Linda H. Chen, Wei Huang, George Jiang
papers.abstract: We examine the role of institutional investors underlying post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD). Our results show that while institutional investors generally herd on earnings news, such correlated trading among institutions does not eliminate or reduce market underreaction to earnings surprises. Instead, PEAD is significant only in the subsample of stocks where institutions herd in the same direction as earnings surprises. In fact, institutional herding is also positively related to next-quarter earnings announcement returns. We provide evidence that institutional herding on or against earnings news is largely driven by firm characteristics, particularly past firm performance and stock returns. In addition, we find that relative to non-transient institutions, transient institutions have a stronger tendency to herd on earnings information. Finally, based on long-run stock returns, we show that when institutions herd on earnings surprises, institutional trading represents a gradual process of incorporating information into stock prices. On the other hand, when institutions herd against earnings surprises, institutional trading slows down stock price discovery.

papers.title: Settlement Speed and Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift: Evidence from the SEC's T+1 Reform
papers.abstract: Post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD) is commonly attributed to limits to arbitrage: sophisticated traders cannot fully correct mispricing when capital is costly to deploy or slow to redeploy. We use the SEC's May 2024 shortening of the standard equity settlement cycle from two days (T+2) to one day (T+1) as a sharp, marketwide shock to the cost of recycling arbitrage capital, and test whether it compressed PEAD. Using approximately 35,000 firm-quarter observations, we find that drift at the shortest post-announcement horizon (3 trading days) compressed significantly after the reform, while drift at longer horizons (5 through 60 days) did not-exactly the horizon-specific pattern a capital-recycling mechanism predicts. This finding survives a battery of checks: a quarter-standardized surprise measure, a clean placebo test using a fake reform date, and a wild cluster bootstrap. We further find that compression is significantly stronger where abnormal volume is high, consistent with faster settlement relaxing market makers' capital constraints specifically where trading activity is elevated. We interpret these findings as evidence that the T+1 reform compressed PEAD through a liquidity/market-making channel, a conclusion relevant both to the limits-to-arbitrage literature and to ongoing settlement-cycle reforms across EU, UK and Switzerland.

papers.title: Post-Earnings Announcement Drift: Evidence from the Corporate Bond Market
papers.authors: Xiaoting Wei, Cameron Truong, Madhu Veeraraghavan
papers.abstract: This study examines the bond pricing behaviour over a 30-day interval subsequent to earnings announcements in the sample period of 2002 – 2010. Our results report a significant and positive relation between bond returns and earnings surprises over the 30-day post-earnings announcement period. In addition, we find that this post-earnings announcement drift is mainly driven by negative earnings news. Bond prices do not exhibit a significant response to positive earnings news. This evidence is consistent with the bond asymmetric payoff function according to Black and Scholes (1973). Furthermore, we examine the impact of bond riskiness on bond price reaction to earnings announcements. We find evidence of a stronger reaction from riskier (speculative-grade) bonds to earnings announcements over the 60-day interval.

papers.title: Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift Prediction: Leveraging Post-event Investor Responses with Multi-task Learning
papers.authors: Yu Zhu, Xiao Liu, Olivia Sheng
papers.abstract: Post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD) refers to the phenomenon in which a company’s stock price tends to drift persistently in response to the information released during the earnings announcement event. Predicting PEAD is of great interest to both investors and researchers because the magnitude of PEAD is economically significant. Whereas decades of studies have explored various approaches to forecasting PEAD, prior research has largely overlooked postevent investor responses—a critical intermediary in the PEAD mechanism—because of the limitations of single-task learning (STL). This study addresses this gap by introducing a multitask learning (MTL) framework that explicitly incorporates investor responses as auxiliary tasks while mitigating look-ahead bias. To further enhance model performance, we propose GradPerp, an adaptive task weighting method that assigns greater weight to auxiliary tasks that contribute diverse and informative training signals. Our model employs a multilevel, multiquery transformer architecture to facilitate cross-task learning, effectively integrating structured financial features with lengthy earnings call transcripts. Evaluation of the model from 2010 to 2022 demonstrates that the proposed design innovations not only outperform benchmark models in terms of prediction accuracy but also generate a daily risk-adjusted return (alpha) two to three times larger than the traditional earnings surprise–based models. This study contributes to the stream of information systems (IS) literature at the intersection of artificial intelligence (AI), finance, and design science research. Our work provides valuable decision support modules and managerial implications for investment and other financial decision makers.

papers.title: Earnings Credibility and Post–Earnings Announcement Drift: Evidence from SPAC Merger and Traditional IPO Firms
papers.authors: Gilbert Nartea, Heeseong Noh, Mona Yaghoubi, Sanghyun Hong

papers.title: Accounting Quality, Liquidity Risk, and Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift
papers.authors: Jeff Zeyun Chen, Gerald J. Lobo, Joseph Zhang
papers.abstract: Building on recent market microstructure research, we decompose liquidity risk into an accounting-associated component and a non-accounting-associated component and examine their relative importance in explaining post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD). We find that the accounting-associated component has a stronger related to PEAD returns than is its non-accounting-associated counterpart, consistent with Sadka (2006)’s suggestion that the information component of liquidity risk is important for explaining PEAD. Results of cross-sectional tests reveal that the relation between accounting-associated liquidity risk and PEAD returns is weaker for firms with greater analyst following. We also find that in a significant market downturn, the relation between accounting-associated liquidity risk and PEAD returns becomes more pronounced.

papers.title: Credit Rating, Post-Earnings - Announcement - Drift, and the Arbitrage
Government Intervention Signals and Post‐Earnings‐Announcement‐Drift: Evidence from China
papers.authors: Yangyang Yu, Xiaoyuan Liu, Zhen Hu

papers.title: Can Social Communication Explain the Decline in Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift?
papers.authors: Yohanes E. Riyanto, Nilanjan Roy, Jiani Wu
papers.abstract: We design a dynamic asset market experiment with exogenous information linkages among investors to study the causal effect of social interaction on post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD). Confirming recent theoretical predictions, we find that trading aggressiveness and price informativeness in the pre-announcement period increase with information linkages. Social interaction improves traders' inference of the fundamental value and enhances the quality of pre-announcement information among individual investors. This results in a weaker response to the public earnings announcement, with the magnitude of PEAD declining in the density of the information linkages. We demonstrate that social connectedness is an important determinant of market efficiency.

papers.title: Macroeconomic Factor Timing
papers.abstract: This paper develops and evaluates a non-parametric timing strategy for five established macroeconomic factor premia: Growth, Inflation, Real Yields, Volatility, and Illiquidity, constructed from survey expectations and standard indicators. Broad index regressions establish the significance of these factors and factor-spanning tests show that each macro factor earns a risk premium that cannot be replicated by the Fama–French–Carhart factors. A similarity-based timing rule, which maps the current macro state to historically analogous periods via Mahalanobis distance, is back-tested from 1990-2023. We first document that the raw timing rule underperforms on both universes: on the CRSP universe over 1990–2023 it yields a cumulative gross return of −12.11% (Sharpe −0.04) versus −15.15% (Sharpe −0.12) for a static equal-weight multi-factor benchmark, and on the S&P 500 it produces −24.78% (Sharpe −0.08) versus +17.20% (Sharpe 0.10). By incorporating two portfolio-construction refinements, volatility targeting (5% annualized target, 24-month lookback) and factor risk parity (24-month lookback), the strategy becomes implementable and scalable, delivering +18.20% (Sharpe 0.13) on CRSP and +17.19% (Sharpe 0.12) on the S&P 500, each outperforming its respective static benchmark, but Sharpe Ratios remain low.

papers.title: When Factor Timing Makes Sense
papers.abstract: In this paper we investigate when it makes sense for portfolio managers to implement factor timing in their quantitative investing, that is we outline necessary circumstances under which the benefits of factor timing (measured by the improvement in Sharpe ratio and the skewness of the returns) outweighs the challenges associated with development and implementation of factor timing. In particular, we mathematically show that factor timing for a single strategy does not yield substantial improvements unless either (1) the Sharpe ratio of the strategy is orders of magnitude different across states, or (2) the signal used for factor timing can accurately predict when the strategy will deliver negative returns (and the portfolio manager is willing to go short the strategy at that time). On the other hand, using simulation, we provide evidence that for a multi-factor portfolio (containing more than 10 factors) allocating risk based on instantaneous correlations between the factors at the beginning of each time period improves performance above the passive approach of allocating risk based on the long-term factor correlations.

papers.title: Factor Loading vs. Factor Timing
Equity Factor Timing With Kalman Filter
papers.abstract: Extensive research literature has shown that equity factor premia is not constant over time. With the broad adoption of factor investing among active managers, to generate differentiated market views and returns, factor or style timing remains as one attractive means. We present an adaptive linear factor model to capture time-varying factor risk premia and discuss its application in equity portfolio investment. The model framework that allows time-varying factor returns can potentially capture more returns and allows an investor to understand the changes in cross-sectional factor returns. We estimate model coefficients through a Kalman filter model and discuss the results with an empirical example.

papers.title: Timing is Money: The Factor Timing Ability of Hedge Fund Managers
papers.authors: Albert Jakob Osinga, Marc Schauten, Remco C.J. Zwinkels
papers.abstract: This paper studies the level, determinants, and implications of the factor timing ability of hedge fund managers. We find that approximately 30% of hedge funds display factor timing ability on at least one factor, concentrated especially at the market, size, and bond factors. Better factor timing skills are related to funds that are more experienced and more flexible. Factor timing is associated with outperformance. Out-of-sample, the top factor timing funds outperform the bottom factor timing funds with a significant 4.32% per annum. Timing skills, though, do not directly lead to higher net flow.

papers.title: Factor Timing with Transaction Costs
papers.abstract: Using a unique dataset of 50 long-short smart beta factors with returns net of transaction costs, we construct a strategy that dynamically invests in factors based on past returns and covariances. The results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms a static 1/N benchmark in terms of risk-adjusted returns, even in the post-2000 period of declining factor premiums. The strategy's low turnover and cost-effective implementation address key practical concerns, providing a robust framework for successful factor timing after transaction costs. The results are robust to multiple specification choices, such as covariance shrinkage, training window length, and transaction cost levels.

papers.title: Factor Investing Lecture 10: Factor Timing and Factor Allocation (Presentation Slides)
papers.abstract: These lecture notes are part of a course of The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen on Factor Investing (DDA3600), offering a comprehensive introduction to the theory and practice of factor-based asset pricing. This lecture examines methods and empirical findings on timing and allocating factors in investment portfolios. It introduces common approaches like valuation spreads, momentum, volatility, investor sentiment, and macroeconomic conditions, discussing their impact on factor performance. Subjective macroeconomic perceptions and financial constraints are highlighted as key drivers of time-varying factor returns, especially for firms with high constraints. Using a Stochastic Discount Factor (SDF) framework, the lecture simplifies factor timing with principal component analysis (PCA). Despite exploring advanced timing strategies, results from the Chinese stock market show that equal-weighted factor portfolios often outperform timing methods, underscoring the challenges and the need for economic reasoning in factor allocation.

papers.title: Factor Timing in the Chinese Stock Market
papers.abstract: I conduct an exploratory study about the feasibility of factor timing in the Chinese stock market, covering 24 representative and well-identified risk factors in ten categories from the literature. The long-short portfolio of short-term reversal exhibits strong and statistically significant out-of-sample predictability, which is robust across various models and all types of predictors. However, such results are not evident in the prediction of all other factors’ long-short portfolios, as well as all factors’ long-wing and short-wing portfolios. The high exposure to the market beta, together with the unpredictability of the market return, explains these failures to some degree. On the other hand, a simple investment strategy based on predicted returns of the reversal factor’s long-short portfolio obtains a significant return three times higher than the simple buy-and-hold strategy in the sample period, with a significant annualized 20.4% CH-3 alpha.

papers.title: Corporate Disclosure Timing Strategy in the Supply Chain
Risk Factor and Liquidity Timing: A Short-Term Approach
papers.abstract: This paper outlines a comprehensive timing approach starting from a conditional model in order to examine daily as well as monthly risk factor timing. Moreover, timing of liquidity risk is explored as evidence on this issue is still missing in the timing literature. This paper considers a Kalman filter approach to introduce time-variation in risk exposures, without having to rely on instrument variables which are often unavailable at a daily frequency. Analyses of timing, conditioning and forecasting abilities of fund managers are simultaneously conducted on a broad set of mutual funds as well as hedge funds. The 2002 to 2009 period considered covers the recent financial market crisis. The findings suggest that there are no daily risk factor timing abilities by the asset managers examined, but that non-plausible evidence of perverse market timing is reduced by moving from unconditional timing tests to a dynamic timing approach. In contrast to the more promising evidence on monthly risk factor timing for mutual and hedge funds, fund managers either do not appropriately react to daily factor information or form false expectations about risk factor performance. Evidence on liquidity timing, whose importance as a risk factor has been emphasized in recent research, is negligibly weak. This also holds for the still novel idiosyncratic risk factor and the widely used Carhart factors. Overall, awareness of fund managers has to be directed to more actively manage dynamics in undiversifiable risk factors.

papers.title: Factor Timing; a Risk and Mispricing Approach
papers.abstract: In this study, we address the key question of whether the drivers of factor returns, namely risk and mispricing, have implications for factor timing strategies. To this end, we propose two factor timing strategies that incorporate risk and mispricing characteristics of style factors, as well as market-wide risk and mispricing state variables. Our chosen predictors include the credit spread and investor sentiment to serve as market-wide risk and mispricing state variables. We also propose a two-factor model consisting the market factor and a common mispricing factor, and style factor risk and mispricing characteristics are defined by style factor sensitivities to these systematic factors. We utilize a parametric approach alongside a scenario-based timing strategy to model the dependence of portfolio weights on these conditioning variables. Both timing strategies achieve significantly higher performance compared to equal-weighting and other benchmark strategies. Our findings underscore that jointly considering risk and mispricing as drivers of factor returns can enhance the effectiveness of factor timing strategies.

papers.title: Factor Timing: At Investors' Own Peril?
papers.authors: Benoit Bellone, Raul Leote de Carvalho

papers.title: Multi-Factor Timing with Deep Learning
papers.authors: Paul Cotturo, Fred Liu, Robert Proner
papers.abstract: We develop deep neural networks with economically motivated restrictions that are designed to overcome the main challenges of factor timing. Our critical innovations include integrating multi-task learning to capture the common structure across factors, with long short-term memory neural networks to extract financial and macroeconomic states. This dynamic multi-task neural network outperforms all benchmarks in terms of predictive accuracy and economic gains. We pinpoint unemployment, along with variations on leverage, profitability, and money as key predictors, and highlight the importance of capturing their nonlinear interactions. Improved factor timing through neural networks with economic restrictions facilitates more reliable investigation into the economic mechanisms driving factor risk premia, and underscores the value of deep learning for factor investing.

papers.title: Avoid Equity Bear Markets with a Market Timing Strategy
papers.abstract: In this paper, our goal is to construct a market timing strategy that would reliably sidestep the equity market during bear markets and thereby reduce market volatility and boost risk-adjusted returns. We build trading signals based on price-based indicators, macroeconomic indicators, and a leading indicator, a yield curve, that can predict recessions and bear markets in advance. Our best-performing strategy uses signals from the Treasury spread, a 200-day SMA, and an alternative risk metric, the Rachev ratio, as trend indicators, while Real Retail Sales Growth, Industrial Production Growth, and Housing Starts Growth as macroeconomic indicators. Based on the sample period from 1927 to 2023, it yields a market-beating annual excess return of 6.59% while nearly doubling the market Sharpe ratio to 0.56 and cutting the maximal drawdown by two-thirds to -25.13%.

papers.title: Non-Fundamental Expectations and Asset Growth Factor Timing
Non-Fundamental Expectations and Asset Growth Factor Timing
Universal Return and Factor Timing
papers.authors: Poh Ling Neo, Chyng Wen Tee, Jeroen Kerkhof

papers.title: Dynamic factor timing approach and its application to the investment portfolios
papers.abstract: This paper is devoted to the dynamic factor timing approach and its application to the investment portfolios

papers.title: Factor Timing Is Not Implementation-Invariant: Selection Authority in Integrated Portfolios
papers.abstract: A factor allocation does not carry the same meaning across portfolio-construction methods. In a sleeve portfolio, a budget allocates capital. In an integrated portfolio, the same number enters a stock-ranking rule and may exert a different influence on which securities are selected. We call that influence selection authority. Using quarterly Russell 1000 portfolios from 2010 through 2026, we find that equal score coefficients produce average authority of 16.2% for quality, 31.8% for value, 28.0% for momentum, and 24.0% for low volatility. Performance, variance, and covariance timing budgets generate different holdings and return increments when implemented through sleeves, breadth-matched consolidation, nominal integration, or authority-matched integration. Matching authority replaces 25%-34% of selected names and raises turnover, while matched comparisons do not show a reliable return benefit. The results separate three institutional decisions: the factor view, the portfolio-construction layer, and the influence granted to each factor over final holdings. Reporting selection authority makes this translation visible and auditable. KEY TAKEAWAYS 1. A factor budget allocates capital in a sleeve portfolio but only enters a stock-selection rule in an integrated portfolio; the same timing decision is not implementation-invariant. 2. Selection authority measures which factor can move stocks across the portfolio boundary. It is empirically distinct from exposure, turnover, return attribution, and risk contribution. 3. Authority matching materially changes holdings and characteristics, raises trading, and does not deliver a reliable return benefit. Institutions should report the translation from factor policy to security selection rather than only nominal score weights.

papers.title: Optimal Factor Timing in a High-Dimensional Setting
papers.authors: Robert Lehnherr, Manan Mehta, Stefan Nagel

papers.title: The VIX is Your FIX: a Flexible Strategy to Timing the Stock Market
papers.abstract: We use the VIX and basic trading behavior to time entry and exit from the market. Our strategy captures 89% of the bottom and 91% from the top (you miss only 11% and 9% from the peak point, respectively). We lay our strategy down in six acts. Act I: the daily average return in the stock market is negative when VIX above 23; then sell if VIX in the way up and exceeds this threshold. Act II: the average daily return during the journey of rising VIX above 23 is -0.6%. Act III: the average daily return during the journey of declining from the peak 0.56%. Act IV: exit (enter) when you have back-to-back two downs (up) days with overall 6% or more. Act V: watch the Federal Reserve rates; exit when rates increase (decrease) during expansion (contraction). Act VII: do not trust oil prices as a predictor for future economic growth since the supply side of oil is highly politicized between OPEC and OPEC+. Collectively: when it comes to transition between bear to bull markets or vice versa, the VIX is your FIX.

papers.title: Acquisition Timing Strategy and Performance During Different Types of Merger Waves
papers.abstract: We examine how delaying entry for acquirers (being later movers) during merger waves can improve their acquisition returns. Previous merger wave research has provided conflicting findings regarding the later mover advantage. We argue the later mover advantage is contingent on the type of merger waves. During expansionary waves, later movers perform better by learning from earlier moving acquirers who have pursued more successful acquisitions, as measured by both market returns and operating performance. However, during contractionary waves, later movers do not derive advantage – instead being earlier movers is more advantageous. This later mover advantage also exists when target distance is higher. Finally, we examine learning by later movers in more detail by demonstrating that they can learn by observing early moving acquirers. Our analyses of merger waves across 11 industries provide support for our arguments.

papers.title: Factor Timing
papers.authors: Valentin Haddad, Serhiy Kozak, Shrihari Santosh

papers.title: Factor Timing with Portfolio Characteristics
papers.authors: Anastasios Kagkadis, Ingmar Nolte, Sandra Nolte (Lechner), Nikolaos Vasilas
papers.abstract: In a factor timing context, academic research has focused on identifying a set of predictors that can explain the dynamics of factor portfolios. We propose an alternative approach for timing factor portfolio returns by exploiting the information from their portfolio characteristics. Different combinations of dimension reduction techniques are employed to independently reduce both the number of predictors and portfolios to predict. Characteristic-based models outperform existing methods in terms of exact predictability, as well as investment performance.

papers.title: Factor Timing Is Not Implementation-Invariant: Selection Authority in Integrated Portfolios
papers.abstract: Discretionary equity investors often describe conviction in factor language: own higherquality companies, avoid paying too much, prefer supportive momentum, and retain a defensive counterweight. Translating those views into an integrated stock ranking is not mechanical. Correlated characteristics and a discrete selection boundary determine how much influence each factor actually has over final holdings. We call that influence selection authority. We propose authority-constrained integration (ACI), a translation rule that brings realized authority closer to the investor's stated factor budget while limiting coefficient displacement and changes in holdings. In quarterly Russell 1000 portfolios from April 2010 through March 2026, equal score coefficients assign average authority of 17.1% to quality, 30.9% to value, 27.6% to momentum, and 24.4% to low volatility. ACI reduces the average authority gap by 10.9-14.0 percentage points while replacing 11.6%-15.4% of nominal integrated holdings. Across three deliberately familiar ways of varying factor conviction, ACI raises annualized log return by 24-32 basis points relative to the same budgets implemented nominally, improves Sharpe ratios by 0.03-0.04, and reduces maximum drawdown by 1.3-3.0 percentage points. The gains are modest and not uniformly significant. The central result is about implementation rather than signal discovery: a factor view can guide a stock portfolio only to the extent that the intended factors retain authority over the securities selected.

papers.title: Factor Timing: Evidence from Mutual Fund Skill
papers.authors: Victor Chen, Gady Jacoby, Lei Lu, Yu Xia
papers.abstract: We examine whether widely used mutual fund skill measures distinguish managers with systematic factor timing ability from those without. Using stock holdings, we construct fund skill gap (FSG), defined as the difference in stock attributes between high-and low-skill funds. FSG predicts subsequent factor returns, most strongly for the value factor (HML). This predictability is concentrated among funds with greater managerial discretion, particularly growth-oriented funds. The results are robust to controlling for fund flows, suggesting these skill measures capture meaningful differences in portfolio positioning through an information channel rather than flow-induced price pressure, identifying funds that pursue factor timing strategies.

papers.title: Timing the Factor Zoo via Deep Visualization
papers.authors: Yuecheng Jia, Junye Li, Vera Zhang, Jiangyu Zhao

papers.title: Overnight Returns as a Market Timing Strategy
The Efficient Cross-Section is Sparse: Factor Timing and the Dimension of the SDF
papers.abstract: Out-of-sample Sharpe ratios in the cross-section of anomaly returns keep rising as principal components with negligible variance are added, an apparent violation of the near-arbitrage restriction that expected returns concentrate on a few systematic sources of risk. I argue that this pattern is a property of the payoff space empirical asset pricing studies rather than of the market it describes. Academic anomaly portfolios are held at constant weights despite predictable variation in both their premia and their risk, and are therefore unconditionally mean-variance inefficient. Applying volatility timing and mean timing to each of 212 anomalies, using only each portfolio's own return history, raises the Sharpe ratio of the large majority. In the resulting efficient cross-section, out-of-sample performance is exhausted by nine principal components, whereas the original cross-section continues to improve through 48. The discount factor built from those few components also prices the cross-section more accurately than the celebrated factor models and than its original-space counterpart, in sample and out-of-sample. Factor proliferation appears to measure unharvested timing rents rather than a large number of distinct sources of compensated risk.

papers.title: Dynamic Hedging, Expected Returns and Factor Timing
Commercialization of Platform Technologies: Launch Timing and Versioning Strategy
papers.authors: Hemant K. Bhargava, Daewon Sun, Byung Cho Kim
papers.abstract: Many emerging entrepreneurial applications and services connect two or more groups of users over Internet-based information technologies. Commercial success of such platform technology products requires adoption of astute business practices related to product line design, price discrimination, and launch timing. We examine these issues for a platform firm that serves two markets, labeled as user and developer markets, with the latter emerging after the user market is proven. While the size of each market positively impacts participation in the other, our model allows for uncertainty regarding developer participation. We demonstrate that product versioning is an especially attractive strategy for platform firms, i.e., the tradeoff between market size and margins is tilted in the direction of more versions. However, when expanding the product line carries substantial fixed costs (e.g., marketing cost, cost of additional plant, managing multiple sets of inventory, increased distribution cost) then the uncertainty in developer participation adversely impacts the firm’s ability to offer multiple versions. We show that for established firms with lower uncertainty about developer participation, the choice is essentially between an expanded or minimal product line. Startups and firms that are entering a new product category are more likely to benefit from a “wait and see” deferred expansion strategy. Still, we demonstrate that uncertainty in developer participation can make early expansion desirable because it expands the installed base and, with the consequent increase in developer participation levels, increases the long-term incremental gain from product line expansion.

papers.title: Decommissioning Strategy and Retirement Timing under Residual Spent Fuel Inventory: The Case of Diablo Canyon
papers.abstract: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission primarily authorizes two decommissioning strategies for retired nuclear power plants, immediate dismantling (DECON) and delayed dismantling (SAFSTOR). Dismantling starts shortly after retirement and completes within 10 years under DECON strategy. In contrast, SAFSTOR allows a maximum 60 years of dormancy period after the retirement of the power plant. The objective of this study is to identify the optimal retirement timing and corresponding decommissioning strategy for nuclear power plants. First, it develops a static cost minimization model based on a predetermined retirement time for identifying the appropriate decommissioning strategy. The study expresses the static model as a function of residual inventory of spent nuclear fuel. It determines the level of residual inventory from a stock-flow accumulation model. Next, the study develops a dynamic optimization model by employing a current value Hamiltonian approach. This dynamic model determines the optimal residual inventory and subsequently derives the corresponding retirement time. The study applies both models to the Diablo Canyon Power Plant (DCPP) of California. The static model identifies a threshold discount rate of 2.98% for DCPP. Any discount rate above this threshold limit makes SAFSTOR more cost-effective compared to DECON. The static model also identifies an optimal dormancy period of 34.21 years for SAFSTOR strategy. The dynamic model reveals that both the optimal residual inventory and retirement timing increase with the plant’s operational profit. These findings highlight the role of discount rate assumptions and profitability conditions for the determination of retirement timing and decommissioning strategy.

papers.title: The Economic Value of Forecasting and Strategy Gains in Volatility Timing
papers.authors: Wen Xu, Pakorn Aschakulporn, Jin E. Zhang
papers.abstract: Existing research suggests that the economic gains from volatility timing stem from covariance forecasting and portfolio construction, yet their relative importance remains unclear. This paper disentangles the contributions of these two channels by jointly evaluating three covariance models, the Dynamic Conditional Correlation Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity model (DCC), the range based Multiplicative Error Model (MEM), and the Multivariate Stochastic Volatility model (MSV), together with three portfolio construction strategies, minimum variance (MIN), maximum return (MAX), and volatility managed (VM). Our results show that the MSV model consistently outperforms DCC and MEM, highlighting the role of stochastic volatility in improving covariance estimation. From a portfolio perspective, both MAX and VM deliver higher economic value than MIN. However, there is no clear evidence that either MAX or VM consistently dominates the other, suggesting that volatility managed strategies do not systematically outperform the standard mean variance framework.

papers.title: Trading Costs and Machine-Learning Return Forecasts
papers.abstract: In a large panel of U.S. stocks, machine-learning return forecasts are most accurate where little capital can be invested. Among stocks that can absorb capital, predictability is weak and hard to estimate precisely. We ask whether trading costs should enter the loss on which the forecast is trained or the way the portfolio is held and traded. Across an elastic net, a boosted tree, and a neural network, reweighting the loss toward liquid stocks does not significantly improve the ordering of those stocks or the net Sharpe ratio, whereas restricting the training sample to liquid stocks lowers accuracy on the stocks it retains. Weighting holdings by liquidity and trading only when the forecast covers the half bid-ask spread raises the net Sharpe ratio of the standard forecast with $500 million of capital invested from -0.38 to 0.42, while the gross Sharpe ratio falls from 1.86 to 1.21; retraining under the reweighted loss adds a statistically negligible 0.12 to the net Sharpe ratio.

papers.title: Cross-Sectional Return Prediction Using Machine Learning: A Practitioner Pipeline
papers.abstract: This paper evaluates three machine learning (ML) modelsRidge Regression, XGBoost, and LightGBMfor cross-sectional equity return prediction using real daily price and volume data for 473 U.S. large-cap stocks over November 2018November 2023, sourced from Yahoo Finance. We implement a strict walk-forward pipeline: training on December 2019December 2021, validating on JanuaryJune 2022, and testing on July 2022October 2023a period spanning the 2022 bear market and 2023 recovery. Ten price-based and liquidity features are constructed with strict no-leakage temporal discipline. Ridge Regression achieves the highest out-of-sample R 2 (0.80%), outperforming XGBoost (0.39%) and LightGBM (0.38%), consistent with linear models performing competitively on short data panels with limited signal-to-noise ratios. All three models generate positive mean Information Coecients (0.0520.058), with XGBoost maintaining the highest proportion of positive-IC months (60%). Long-short quintile portfolios yield net annualised Sharpe ratios of 0.66 (Ridge), 0.80 (XGBoost), and 1.49 (Light-GBM) after 15 bps transaction costs. The Deated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) framework reveals that no model achieves DSR > 1.0 under the 16-month test windowa nding driven by the short sample length rather than absence of predictive contentwith Light-GBM nearest at DSR = 0.985. Volatility features (retvol60, retvol20) dominate feature importance across all three architectures, followed by 12-month momentum. All data and results are fully reproducible from freely available Yahoo Finance data using the provided pipeline.

papers.title: Choices Matter When Training Machine Learning Models For Return Prediction
papers.abstract: Applying machine learning to cross-sectional stock return prediction requires careful consideration of modeling choices. Common approaches that fail to account for heterogeneity or imbalanced stock representation in training data can lead to suboptimal performance. I study two strategies to address these issues: training group-specific models and predicting relative returns. Both approaches yield similar economic improvements over models trained on the full cross-section of U.S. stock returns, with value-weighted trading strategies benefiting significantly. The findings underscore the importance of aligning machine learning modeling decisions with desired economic outcomes and provide guidance for researchers and practitioners seeking robust machine learning models.

papers.title: Asset Return Prediction via Machine Learning
The Prediction Paradox: Why Machine Learning Models Fail to Predict Cryptocurrency Prices in Live Trading
papers.abstract: A growing body of literature claims high accuracy in cryptocurrency price prediction using machine learning models, with reported backtest accuracies ranging from 85% to 99%. However, these claims are almost exclusively validated through historical backtesting, with live trading results conspicuously absent. This paper presents a rare empirical study of three sequentially-developed ML-based trading systems deployed on Binance ETHUSDC perpetual futures over a three-month period (January-April 2026).
